programs.name: Artificial Intelligence
programs.fullName: Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence and Computational Science — Graduate-Style Self-Study Program
programs.description: Harvard’s CSE master’s is an interdisciplinary Computational Science and Engineering degree, not an AI MS. Harvard says it joins computer science, applied mathematics, and engineering sciences; emphasizes modeling/simulation, parallel programming/collaborative software, and large-data methods; and lists ten outcomes including computational framing, reproducible analysis, parallel/distributed computing, maintainable artifacts, and enabling a domain breakthrough. The on-campus SM is eight courses; the ME adds a thesis year. This self-study program adapts those outcomes into a broader 14-course AI/CS sequence rather than claiming equivalence, credit, admission, or a Harvard degree.

prerequisites.bridge_required: AI-B01 and AI-B02 are explicit, non-credit prerequisite bridges. Learners already competent in Python, linear algebra, algorithms, probability, and calculus may pass by completing the bridge assessments at ≥70%, but should still use the linked materials to close gaps.
prerequisites.diagnostic: Before AI-G01, demonstrate: Python testing/file I/O; SVD/least squares; Big-O/proof basics; conditional probability/Bayes/expectation; derivatives/gradient descent. Complete remedial units before proceeding, rather than treating advanced courses as a substitute for foundations.
prerequisites.undergraduate_vs_graduate: AI-B01 and AI-B02 are labeled undergraduate prerequisite bridge. AI-G01 deliberately uses MIT 6.036 as a transition; the CS50 AI recap is an undergraduate substitute, not claimed graduate credit. AI-G02 through AI-G12 are graduate-style in prerequisite depth, proof/experiment expectations, and substantive work.

schedule.pace: Part-time: one course at a time, 12–15 h/week. Schedule 10–12 weeks for 150–190 h courses and 8–10 weeks for 100–140 h courses; take a one-week consolidation break between terms.
sequence: Year 4 (first half): AI-G11, AI-G12, then a 180-hour capstone synthesis.
schedule.duration: Approximately 3.25–3.75 years at 12–15 h/week including consolidation and an additional 180 capstone hours; course hours sum to 2,230 and the program total includes the incremental capstone allocation.

capstone.title: Reproducible, Responsible AI/CSE Capstone
capstone.brief: Frame a real scientific, engineering, or public-interest problem; compare a mechanistic/numerical or algorithmic baseline with an ML/AI approach; document data rights; evaluate uncertainty, subgroup/shift behavior, compute/cost, and deployment risks; and publish a reproducible repository, 12–15 page report, 10-minute recorded presentation, model/system card, and governance memo.
milestones: Problem and stakeholder brief with success/failure criteria.
Protocol and baseline before model selection.
Final artifact, audit, and oral defense to two technically literate reviewers.
capstone.completion_rubric: Technical soundness 30%; evaluation and uncertainty 20%; reproducibility/software quality 20%; responsible-AI and governance analysis 15%; communication/domain relevance 15%. Pass at 70%, with no score below 60% in reproducibility or responsible-AI dimensions.

programs.accessNotes: No enrollment or payment is required for the linked public materials unless a provider changes access. Do not submit work to a course platform unless you independently choose to create an account. Videos are linked, not downloaded. MIT OCW materials are used under MIT OCW terms; author/publisher permissions are recorded per textbook. Paid, login-only, and copyrighted case material is excluded.
limitations: This is a self-study design, not a degree, certificate, transfer-credit plan, or representation of Harvard/MIT/Stanford/Berkeley affiliation. Harvard CSE itself is not an AI MS; it is CSE centered on mathematical/computational foundations, modeling/simulation, parallel computing, and data analysis.

Verified runtime is a conservative, deduplicated lower bound from 132 individually visible public timecodes across three actual course playlists. Planned watch hours elsewhere are study allocations, not claims about video runtime.

Several official or university course pages expose per-lecture videos without public aggregate durations, and a few specialty areas lack a matching full graduate video archive. Those entries explicitly say planned only and name the topic gap rather than inventing runtime or complete coverage.
The CS224N ledger excludes three visible playlist items whose timecodes were not captured. Its 25.174167 hours is a lower bound, not the claimed duration of all 23 videos.

Some author-provided complete book PDFs (Jurafsky/Martin and Sutton/Barto) are linked but not stored locally because bounded legal downloads did not complete. Szeliski’s official page requires completion of a personal-use download form; it was not automated.
Local PDFs were verified by their %PDF magic bytes. They are reference copies, not a redistribution grant; consult every source page for current terms and attribution.

For reliable public access, AI-G02 uses the complete undergraduate 6.046J recording sequence with graduate 6.854 readings; AI-G05 uses the complete graduate 18.086 sequence with 18.335J readings. These substitutions are not claims that the original degree lectures are all open.

programs.name: Business Administration
programs.fullName: Harvard MBA-Inspired Business Administration — Open Self-Study Program
programs.description: The current HBS MBA curriculum page lists a common first-year Required Curriculum and FIELD: FIN1, FRC, LEAD, MKT, TOM, STRAT, DSAIL, BGIE, TEM, FIN2, LCA, and Purpose of the Firm. This self-study design maps every named area, combines LCA and Purpose into one integrated course, adds two electives, and ends in a FIELD-style capstone. The HBS catalog search also currently exposes ten academic units, including Finance, Marketing, Organizational Behavior, Strategy, Technology and Operations Management, Entrepreneurial Management, and BGIE.
prerequisites: High-school algebra, percentages, and graph reading.
Spreadsheet fluency (formulas, tables, charts); learn basic R or Python before MBA-107.
Professional writing and willingness to cite sources.
For the capstone, a lawful project sponsor or independently scoped public-interest project; informed consent for interviews/data.

schedule.format: 24-month, part-time sequence; approximately 11 study hours per week on average (1,135 total planned study hours across 104 weeks). Video is only one component.
sequence: Months 10–12: MBA-112 and MBA-113; complete comprehensive review.
Months 13–24: MBA-114 capstone, with monthly mentor/peer review and final presentation.
completion_criteria: Finish all assigned lecture-series units and readings.
Earn at least 70/100 on every course rubric; revise work below threshold.
Maintain a source log and calculation/code appendix where applicable.
Complete the capstone with a real decision owner or a transparently self-scoped public-interest project, plus feedback and reflection.
Do not represent completion as an HBS MBA or any university credential.

capstone.deliverable: Sponsor-facing 12–15 page executive report, analysis/model annex, implementation artifact, 10-minute presentation, feedback record, and reflection.
integrative_requirements: data/AI or decision-analysis element where appropriate

programs.accessNotes: This is not an HBS, Harvard, MIT, Yale, Stanford, IIT, NPTEL, or edX degree, certificate, enrollment, or credit-bearing program. No account enrollment, paid purchase, copyrighted case download, or video download was performed. HBS public pages explain the curriculum but do not provide an open, full MBA or a lawful public set of HBS cases. MIT OCW, Yale Open Courses, OpenStax, NPTEL/IIT, and Stanford/YouTube resources are clearly labeled substitutions. HarvardX/edX links are optional supplements only; their stated free-audit availability can change and they were not counted in the video ledger.
limitations: Public HBS materials do not make a full MBA degree or paid/proprietary HBS case collection openly available; none is reproduced or scraped here.

Many primary video sources are undergraduate or external professional courses. Each is labeled as a substitute; the MBA-level work is supplied by assignments, synthesis, and capstone rather than asserted institutional equivalence.

The 47.3528 verified hours are deliberately conservative: only two distinct Yale series are counted, using terminal transcript chapter timestamps rather than class-contact claims or estimates. Other planned video hours are not verified runtime.
The FIELD-style capstone cannot reproduce HBS faculty sponsorship, cohort, global immersion, or company access. It requires learner-arranged ethical project access.

Open course availability, free-audit terms, playlists, and URLs can change. NPTEL syllabus PDFs are short course documents; the substantial local references are the two complete OpenStax textbooks and MIT’s 49-page notes.
The startup recording playlist contains one unavailable item; 19 visible full lectures are linked, with the gap explicitly recorded. Its runtime is not used for the 36-hour minimum.

programs.name: Quantitative Finance
programs.fullName: MIT Master of Finance–Inspired Quantitative Finance
programs.description: The official MIT Sloan MFin curriculum identifies required core work in Foundations of Modern Finance; Financial Mathematics or Advanced Financial Mathematics for Financial Engineering; Programming for Finance Professionals; Corporate Financial Accounting; Finance Ethics & Regulation; Corporate Finance; Financial Markets; Analytics of Finance or Advanced Analytics of Finance; Communications; and at least one Action Learning course. Its restricted electives include Financial Engineering, Consumer Finance and Fintech, Advanced Data Analytics and Machine Learning in Finance, AI and Money, Options and Futures Markets, Fixed Income Securities and Derivatives, Mergers, Acquisitions, and Private Equity, among others. This independent curriculum maps those named components to public materials/substitutes and does not claim equivalence, credit, or access to enrollment-only components.
prerequisites: Calculus (including basic derivatives/integrals), linear algebra, and introductory probability.
Comfort with algebra, spreadsheets, and written quantitative argument.
Python is strongly recommended. If needed, complete the optional free Harvard CS50P bridge: https://cs50.harvard.edu/python/weeks/ (Weeks 0–6 before or alongside MFIN-102).
A public/synthetic data source and a local environment for spreadsheets and Python; no brokerage account is needed or requested.

terms: Months 10–13: MFIN-113 capstone, with a mentor/peer review every four weeks.
schedule.pace: About 20 study hours/week averaged over 52 weeks; adjust down by extending the capstone rather than skipping validation and feedback.

capstone.deliverable: Sponsor-facing 15–20 page report, reproducible code/model annex, data/provenance sheet, risk-and-ethics review, 10-minute presentation, and feedback log.
integrative_requirements: accounting or corporate-finance context where relevant
asset-pricing, fixed-income, derivatives, or risk analysis as appropriate

programs.accessNotes: All resources are lawful public university/open-education or author-hosted materials. MIT OCW courses are archived offerings and are not represented as all current MFin degree lectures. This guide provides no MIT enrollment, degree, certificate, academic credit, professional designation, legal advice, or authorization to trade. Do not upload confidential data; use public, synthetic, or permissioned datasets. No pirated HBS cases, commercial textbook PDFs, or paywalled course materials are used.
limitations: This is curriculum inspiration, not the MIT Master of Finance. It conveys no degree, academic credit, certificate, access to MIT services, or professional credential.

The official core’s Communications course and the three Action Learning options (Investment Management Lab, Corporate Finance/Investment Banking/Private Equity proseminar, and Finance Lab) rely on MIT enrollment, teams, industry practitioners, coaching, and evaluation. MFIN-112 embeds communication practice and MFIN-113 is only a transparent self-directed analogue.

MIT’s official curriculum page is used as the outline; public materials are archived MIT OCW courses or external free substitutes. No claim is made that all current MFin lectures, assignments, faculty interaction, recruiting, grading, or Action Learning experiences are public or replicated.

The verified video floor is deliberately limited to two independently timed full series: 18.650 (28.0122 h) and 15.S08 (13.9225 h), totaling 41.9347 h. Yale Financial Markets is linked but deliberately excluded; 15.071’s 193 short assets totaling 16.1464 h are also excluded from the floor.
Planned video hours are scheduling estimates except the two ledger entries. Reused supporting series may appear in several courses but never increase verified hours more than once.
University readings may change or move. Respect each host’s license/terms; local copies are retained only where supplied and are not a license grant.
Assignments are educational simulations. They are not investment recommendations, offers, solicitations, legal/compliance advice, or instructions to transact.

Full Stanford optimization and IIT Madras econometrics recordings replace Analytics Edge short clips as the primary video courses. Topic-specific finance extensions are self-study readings/projects. Only MIT statistics and fintech full lectures remain counted in the conservative 41.9347-hour floor.

programs.name: Technology Leadership
programs.description: The official MIT Professional Education CTO outline is a 12-month non-degree professional certificate for experienced leaders. Its five courses are Innovative Leadership: Cultivating Impactful Culture; Management of Technology: Roadmapping and Development; Management of Technology: Strategy and Portfolio Analysis; Applied AI for Digital Transformation; and Applied Agentic AI for Organizational Transformation. It foregrounds technological foresight, AI in the enterprise, R&D/portfolio strategy, and data-driven leadership; its course topics explicitly include responsible AI, cybersecurity/agent risks, portfolio evaluation and finance, and an impact project.

prerequisites.required: Comfort reading technical/business English; 8–11 hours weekly; a workstation with browser, spreadsheet, and diagramming tool; a real or simulated organization for assignments.
prerequisites.technical: For CTO-02, undergraduate systems/networking and programming are expected; MIT 6.033 material is the recommended prerequisite substitute. For CTO-04, introductory linear algebra/calculus and Python are helpful. CTO-03 is deliberately introductory/practitioner-level.
prerequisites.distinction: Courses marked “graduate core” use graduate MIT course materials. CTO-03 is a prerequisite/substitute security literacy module, CTO-04 is technical graduate-core-adjacent literacy, and CTO-09 is an advanced non-credit governance companion. These labels do not confer academic credit.

schedule.length: 42 weeks (about 9.5–10 months) at 8–11 hours/week; 388 planned total study hours.
sequence: Weeks 5–10: CTO-02 cloud-scale architecture and resilience.
Weeks 11–14: CTO-03 cyber and privacy risk.
Weeks 15–19: CTO-04 AI and agentic transformation.
Weeks 20–23: CTO-05 innovation and product strategy.
Weeks 32–37: CTO-08 finance and capital allocation.
Weeks 38–42: CTO-09 governance, integration, and capstone.
schedule.weekly_pattern: Reserve 60–70% for primary lectures/reading and 30–40% for the listed artifact. Keep a decision log that feeds the capstone; do not accelerate by treating provider workload estimates as verified video time.

capstone.title: CTO Technology Strategy and Governance Impact Project
capstone.brief: Choose one organization or a well-specified hypothetical. Deliver a 15–20 page executive dossier plus a 12-slide board presentation. Integrate the CTO-01 roadmap, CTO-02 target architecture, CTO-03 cyber charter, CTO-04 AI dossier, CTO-05 product thesis, CTO-06 change plan, CTO-07 operations plan, CTO-08 capital allocation, and CTO-09 governance gates.
required_sections: Strategic thesis, technology foresight, and roadmap with figures of merit.
Target architecture, resilience posture, data/AI system boundaries, and technical-debt decisions.
R&D/product portfolio, customer value, experiments, and staged investment logic.
Operating model, talent/change plan, decision rights, and delivery/operations KPIs.
Cybersecurity, privacy, AI risk, testing, monitoring, and incident/exception governance.
Financial case with scenarios, sensitivities, assumptions, stop/scale gates, and residual risk.
Board-ready recommendation with accountable owners and 30/90/180-day milestones.
capstone.rubric: Strategic coherence and evidence 25%; architecture/operations feasibility 20%; AI, cyber, and governance rigor 20%; financial discipline 15%; leadership/change execution 10%; clarity of board communication 10%.
capstone.completion_criteria: Complete all nine substantive assignments, retain a lecture/watch log, achieve at least 80/100 on each self-rubric and the capstone, and document revisions from one peer or mentor review. This establishes self-study completion only; it does not create any credential.

programs.accessNotes: This is an independent, no-enrollment self-study companion. It is professional-certificate-inspired and is NOT a master’s degree, MIT course enrollment, MIT Professional Education certificate, or academic credit. MIT OCW says materials can be browsed without signup and are generally shared under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, subject to item-specific notices. Harvard CS50 course material is free to work through; edX enrollment is optional for feedback/certificates. No paid HBS cases, copyrighted course packs, paywalled readings, or downloaded videos are used.
limitations: The companion is independent self-study and awards no degree, MIT certificate, CEU, credit, enrollment, instructor feedback, or alumni access.

courses.title: Python Software Practice Bridge
courses.level: Undergraduate prerequisite bridge
courses.prerequisites: None; CS50P is designed for learners with or without prior experience. Complete before AI-G01.
objectives: Write idiomatic Python using functions, types, control flow, files, and exceptions.
Design tests and debug failures with a disciplined workflow.
Use packages, regular expressions, classes, and data files responsibly.
Produce a small documented, reproducible command-line analysis tool.
units: Weeks 1–2: functions, variables, conditionals, loops, and style.
Weeks 3–4: exceptions, unit testing, file I/O, and debugging.
Weeks 5–6: regular expressions, third-party packages, and command-line workflows.
Weeks 7–8: classes, a final project, README, tests, and a reproducible environment file.
courses.assignment: Build a tested Python package that ingests a public CSV, validates it, produces a clean analysis artifact, and includes a 2-page engineering note.
courses.assessment: Rubric: correctness and tests 35%; decomposition/style 25%; data validation and errors 20%; documentation/reproducibility 20%. Pass threshold: 70%.
courses.mapping: Harvard outcome 3 (usable computational solution), 7 (reproducible analysis), and 9 (robust, maintainable software). This is a prerequisite bridge, not graduate credit.

remainingGaps: Unit 4: No verified free full university lecture in the checked primary series (or targeted follow-up) explicitly covers writing a project README and rebuilding an isolated Python environment from a dependency file such as requirements.txt. courses.title: Mathematical and Algorithmic Readiness Bridge
courses.level: Undergraduate prerequisite bridge
courses.prerequisites: AI-B01 or equivalent programming. Calculus is assumed; complete the diagnostic before starting.
objectives: Manipulate vector spaces, linear maps, least squares, eigensystems, SVD, and positive-definite matrices.
Analyze asymptotic complexity and write a correctness argument for a basic algorithm.
Apply probability axioms, conditional probability, Bayes’ rule, expectations, and distributions.
Connect matrix conditioning, probability, and algorithmic cost to ML modeling choices.
units: Weeks 1–3: complete 18.06 systems, subspaces, rank, orthogonality, and least squares.
Weeks 4–5: eigenvalues, diagonalization, positive definiteness, SVD, and conditioning.
Weeks 6–8: use MIT 6.006 lectures 1–11 for asymptotics, data structures, graphs, and proof patterns.
Weeks 9–10: use 6.041SC for axioms, conditional probability, random variables, expectation, and Bayes.
Weeks 11–12: solve a diagnostic set linking least squares, sampling, and algorithmic complexity.
courses.assignment: Write a short proof portfolio (three correctness/complexity proofs), derive least squares and ridge normal equations, and implement a numerically stable SVD-based regression comparison.
courses.assessment: Rubric: mathematical derivations 35%; proof rigor 25%; correct implementation/experiments 25%; interpretation of conditioning and uncertainty 15%. Pass threshold: 70%.
courses.mapping: Harvard outcomes 1–2 (computational framing and method choice) and 6 (model systems with attention to data and efficiency). This is prerequisite/substitute content, not graduate credit.

unitMap.text: Weeks 1–3: complete 18.06 systems, subspaces, rank, orthogonality, and least squares.
viewingSequence: Start with 18.06 lectures 1–10 for systems, spaces, rank, independence, basis, and the four fundamental subspaces.
Continue with 18.06 lectures 14–17 for orthogonality, projections, least-squares fitting, and Gram–Schmidt.
Use lecture 12 as an optional graph/incidence-matrix application of rank and subspaces.
coveredTopics: systems of linear equations and elimination
unitMap.practicalWork: The assigned problem sets and derivations remain learner work; lecture viewing does not replace them.

unitMap.text: Weeks 4–5: eigenvalues, diagonalization, positive definiteness, SVD, and conditioning.
viewingSequence: Watch 18.06 lectures 21–22 for eigenvalues and diagonalization.
Watch 18.06 lectures 25 and 27 for symmetric and positive-definite matrices.
Watch 18.06 lecture 29 and lecture 33 for SVD and pseudoinverse.
Finish with MIT 18.065 lectures 9–10 for least-squares solution choices, ill-conditioning, error amplification, and regularization.
coveredTopics: conditioning, ill-conditioned systems, and amplification of errors
unitMap.practicalWork: Compare solution methods and numerical behavior in the assigned implementation; video examples are not a substitute for the learner’s experiment.

unitMap.text: Weeks 6–8: use MIT 6.006 lectures 1–11 for asymptotics, data structures, graphs, and proof patterns.
viewingSequence: Follow MIT 6.006 lectures 1–5 for computational modeling, data structures, sorting, and hashing.
Continue with lectures 6–8 for balanced trees and heaps.
Finish with lectures 9–11 for breadth-first search, depth-first search, and weighted shortest paths.
coveredTopics: algorithmic problem framing and correctness/cost analysis
asymptotic growth and algorithmic efficiency foundations
arrays, sets, sorting, hashing, trees, and heaps
graph search and weighted shortest paths
unitMap.practicalWork: Write the required correctness and complexity proofs yourself; the series teaches methods but does not create the course proof portfolio.

unitMap.text: Weeks 9–10: use 6.041SC for axioms, conditional probability, random variables, expectation, and Bayes.
viewingSequence: Start with lectures 1–3 for probability models, axioms, conditioning, Bayes’ rule, and independence.
Watch lectures 5–9 for discrete and continuous random variables and joint distributions.
Watch lectures 10–12 for derived distributions, continuous Bayes, covariance, and iterated expectation.
Use lectures 21–22 as a final Bayesian inference extension.
coveredTopics: conditional probability, Bayes’ rule, and independence
discrete and continuous random variables and distributions
unitMap.practicalWork: Work the probability exercises and sampling calculations; the videos explain the material but do not complete the diagnostic set.

unitMap.text: Weeks 11–12: solve a diagnostic set linking least squares, sampling, and algorithmic complexity.
viewingSequence: Review 18.06 lecture 16 and 18.065 lecture 9 for least-squares fitting and solution alternatives.
Review 6.041 lectures 2, 8, and 12 for conditional probability/Bayes, distributions, and expectation relevant to sampling.
Review MIT 6.006 lectures 1 and 19 for algorithmic analysis and complexity; consult 18.065 lecture 10 for conditioning and regularization.
Use MIT 6.036 lecture 5 to connect regression and ridge regularization to a supervised-learning modeling choice.
Then solve the original integrated diagnostic set independently.
coveredTopics: probability, sampling-related distributions, and expectation foundations
algorithm analysis and computational cost foundations
linear regression and ridge regularization as a modeling choice
uncoveredTopics: No verified public lecture integrates least squares, sampling/probability, conditioning, algorithmic complexity, and model choice into the specific cross-domain diagnostic required by this unit; the component lectures are partial support, not a complete substitute.
unitMap.practicalWork: The course-specific diagnostic set is learner work. It must be completed directly; watching these videos does not satisfy it. The required proof portfolio, derivations, and numerically stable SVD-vs-regression implementation likewise remain learner work.

remainingGaps: No verified public lecture integrates least squares, sampling/probability, conditioning, algorithmic complexity, and model choice into the specific cross-domain diagnostic required by this unit; the component lectures are partial support, not a complete substitute.

objectives: Implement search and constraint-based reasoning.
Use probability and Bayesian reasoning in intelligent systems.
Implement optimization, classification and neural-network baselines.
Explain language models and evaluate an AI project with tests.
units: Week 0: Search; implement Degrees and Tic-Tac-Toe.
Week 1: Knowledge; implement Knights and Minesweeper.

Week 4: Learning; implement Shopping and Nim.

courses.assignment: Complete all named official projects with your own code, tests and a reflection explaining at least one failure case per week. Do not use answer repositories.

courses.mapping: Harvard CS50/HarvardX AI pathway; preparation for the AI graduate-style core, not Harvard CSE degree credit.

courses.title: Machine Learning: Modeling, Generalization, and AI Foundations
courses.level: Graduate core (uses CS50 AI only as an undergraduate substitute in Unit 1)
courses.prerequisites: AI-B01 and AI-B02. Before Unit 2, complete the CS50 AI search/classification recap if not already familiar with it.
objectives: State a learning problem with explicit population, target, loss, hypothesis class, and evaluation protocol.
Derive and implement linear classifiers, regression, kernel methods, and basic neural networks.
Diagnose overfitting, data leakage, calibration, and distribution shift.
Compare models with uncertainty-aware, reproducible experiments.
Explain how search, classification, optimization, and LLM concepts from CS50 AI connect to formal ML.
units: Unit 1: CS50 AI recap—search, classification, optimization, and the project style.
Units 2–3: representations, perceptrons, feature engineering, margins, and losses.
Units 4–5: regression, regularization, kernels, and validation.
Units 6–7: neural networks, backpropagation, and representation learning.
Units 8–9: probabilistic modeling, temporal data, RL preview, and an experiment audit.
courses.assignment: Choose a public classification or regression dataset. Implement a baseline and two model families, pre-register the split/metrics, run an ablation, and submit a 6-page reproducible report.
courses.assessment: Rubric: problem formulation/data audit 20%; correct models 25%; evaluation and uncertainty 25%; ablation/interpretation 20%; reproducible repository 10%. Pass threshold: 70%.
courses.mapping: Harvard outcomes 1–3, 6–7, and 9: formulate a prediction problem, compare approaches, reproduce an analysis, and produce maintainable code.

courses.assignment: Select an AI/CSE workload (routing, batching, retrieval, or allocation). Prove a bound for a proposed algorithm, implement it, and benchmark against a justified baseline.
courses.assessment: Rubric: formal model and proof 35%; implementation correctness 20%; benchmark design 20%; limitations/counterexamples 15%; research-style exposition 10%. Pass threshold: 70%.

courses.title: Probabilistic Modeling and Statistical Inference
courses.level: Graduate core
courses.prerequisites: AI-B02 and AI-G01; multivariable calculus and linear algebra.
objectives: Construct probability spaces, conditional models, and Bayesian updates.
Derive estimators, likelihoods, confidence/credible intervals, and posterior-predictive checks.
Use graphical-model reasoning for latent variables and temporal sequences.
Assess calibration, uncertainty, and the limits of probabilistic assumptions in ML.
units: Weeks 1–2: axioms, conditional probability, Bayes, and random variables.
Weeks 3–4: distributions, expectation, variance, LLN, and CLT.
Weeks 5–6: estimation, hypothesis testing, and likelihood.
Weeks 7–8: multivariate models, Gaussian inference, and regression uncertainty.
Weeks 9–10: Markov chains, HMMs, and Bayesian networks.
Weeks 11–12: calibration, posterior prediction, and a reproducible inference study.
courses.assignment: Build a Bayesian or likelihood-based model for a real dataset; conduct prior sensitivity, posterior-predictive checks, calibration evaluation, and a comparison with a discriminative baseline.
courses.assessment: Rubric: model assumptions/derivation 30%; valid inference implementation 25%; diagnostics and uncertainty 25%; communication of limitations 20%. Pass threshold: 70%.
courses.mapping: Harvard outcomes 1–2, 6–7, and 10: model uncertainty, choose a suitable computational approach, and use reproducible data analysis.

unitMap.text: Weeks 1–2: axioms, conditional probability, Bayes, and random variables.
viewingSequence: M641-001: axioms; M641-005: conditioning and Bayes; M641-009: independence; M641-017 then M641-020: discrete random variables, PMFs and expectations.
coveredTopics: Probability models and axioms / probability spaces
Discrete random variables, probability mass functions and expectation
unitMap.practicalWork: Videos support derivations; complete the course problem sets and assigned dataset modeling independently.

unitMap.text: Weeks 3–4: distributions, expectation, variance, LLN, and CLT.
viewingSequence: M641-017, 020, 024, 026: discrete then continuous distributions and expectations; M641-031, 041, 044: joint/derived distributions, covariance and iterated expectations; M641-062 then M641-066: weak law then central limit theorem.
coveredTopics: Discrete and continuous distributions, PMFs/CDFs and derived distributions
Expectation, variance, covariance and iterated expectation
Weak law of large numbers and convergence in probability
Central limit theorem and probability bounds
unitMap.practicalWork: Worked recitations are instructional examples, not a replacement for independent problem solving.

unitMap.text: Weeks 5–6: estimation, hypothesis testing, and likelihood.
viewingSequence: M641-069–073: Bayesian statistical inference, parameter inference and worked example; M641-074–076: classical statistical inference sequence; MPI-PPC-L5: Bayesian hypothesis testing and posterior predictive checks.
unitMap.practicalWork: Watching methods does not complete the required model fit, sensitivity analysis, diagnostics or baseline comparison.

unitMap.text: Weeks 7–8: multivariate models, Gaussian inference, and regression uncertainty.
viewingSequence: M641-030: normal probability calculations; M641-031, 035, 041: multivariate continuous distributions, continuous Bayes/derived distributions and covariance; MIT6S191-L10: ML predictive uncertainty/calibration as a partial bridge.
coveredTopics: General predictive uncertainty and calibration concepts for deep-learning predictions
uncoveredTopics: Gaussian parameter or linear-regression inference with regression-specific uncertainty intervals is not directly taught by these recordings.
unitMap.practicalWork: MIT 6.438 notes offer a non-video reference for Gaussian graphical models; they do not count as viewed lectures.

unitMap.text: Weeks 9–10: Markov chains, HMMs, and Bayesian networks.
viewingSequence: M641-056–060: Markov-chain lectures in order; M641-057–058 and 061: optional worked examples. MIT 6.438 notes are a non-video fallback for HMMs and graphical inference.
coveredTopics: Markov-chain construction, transition behavior and related Markov-process analysis
uncoveredTopics: Hidden Markov models and latent-state inference lack a verified public lecture in the assembled inventory.
Bayesian networks / directed probabilistic graphical models lack a verified public lecture in the assembled inventory.
unitMap.practicalWork: MIT 6.438 is a non-video fallback for deeper graphical-inference notes, not a direct playable lecture.

unitMap.text: Weeks 11–12: calibration, posterior prediction, and a reproducible inference study.
viewingSequence: M641-069–070, 073: Bayesian inference examples; M641-074–076: classical comparison; MIT6S191-L10: uncertainty/calibration/distribution shift; MPI-PPC-L5: Bayesian hypothesis tests and posterior predictive checks.
coveredTopics: Bayesian and classical inference background relevant to posterior prediction
Predictive uncertainty, confidence calibration and calibration error
unitMap.practicalWork: Learners must still build and document a reproducible Bayesian/likelihood model on real data, test prior sensitivity, run posterior-predictive checks, evaluate calibration, compare a discriminative baseline and write limitations; videos replace none of this work.

courses.title: Convex and First-Order Optimization for AI
courses.level: Graduate core
courses.prerequisites: AI-B02 and AI-G03; linear algebra, probability, calculus, and basic Python.
objectives: Recognize convex sets, functions, and disciplined convex programs.
Derive optimality conditions, dual problems, and certificates.
Implement least squares, regularized regression, constrained optimization, and first-order methods.
Explain optimization failure modes, conditioning, and tradeoffs in ML training.
units: Weeks 1–2: convex sets/functions and modeling examples.
Weeks 3–4: least squares, LP/QP, Lagrange multipliers, and duality.
Weeks 5–6: interior-point and first-order methods; CVXPY practice.
Weeks 7–8: regularization, sparse recovery, robust objectives, and ML applications.
Weeks 9–10: optimization audit of a training or allocation problem.
courses.assignment: Formulate and solve a constrained ML/CSE design problem in CVXPY; derive its dual, validate KKT residuals, and compare a first-order solver with a closed-form or baseline method.
courses.assessment: Rubric: formulation/derivation 35%; correct computational solution 25%; numerical validation 20%; interpretation and modeling caveats 20%. Pass threshold: 70%.
courses.mapping: Harvard outcomes 2, 6, 7, and 9: choose efficient methods, model constraints, reproduce numerical results, and write reliable computational artifacts.

lectures.title: Stanford EE364A Convex Optimization I Stephen Boyd I 2023 I Lecture 1
lectures.coverageNote: Course opening plus introductory optimization examples: least squares, linear programming, convex optimization, and application framing; keep the math/application chapters, not just course administration.

lectures.title: Stanford EE364A Convex Optimization I Stephen Boyd I 2023 I Lecture 2
lectures.coverageNote: Affine and convex sets, convex hulls/cones, hyperplanes and halfspaces, norm balls, polyhedra, PSD cone, intersections, generalized inequalities, and minimum/minimal elements.

lectures.title: Stanford EE364A Convex Optimization I Stephen Boyd I 2023 I Lecture 3
lectures.coverageNote: Generalized inequalities and separation, convex functions, first/second-order conditions, least-squares quadratics, epigraphs, Jensen's inequality, and convexity rules.

lectures.title: Stanford EE364A Convex Optimization I Stephen Boyd I 2023 I Lecture 4
lectures.coverageNote: Constructive convexity; pointwise maximum, supremum and composition rules; perspective and conjugate functions; quasiconvex functions.

lectures.title: Stanford EE364A Convex Optimization I Stephen Boyd I 2023 I Lecture 5
lectures.coverageNote: Convex optimization problem forms, local/global optimality, feasibility and implicit constraints, optimality criterion, equivalent problems, and quasiconvex optimization.

lectures.title: Stanford EE364A Convex Optimization I Stephen Boyd I 2023 I Lecture 6
lectures.coverageNote: Named problem classes and modeling: LP, QP, QCQP, SOCP, robust LP, geometric programming, and optimization examples.

lectures.title: Stanford EE364A Convex Optimization I Stephen Boyd I 2023 I Lecture 7
lectures.coverageNote: Generalized inequality constraints, semidefinite programs, vector/multicriterion optimization, Pareto tradeoffs, scalarization, and portfolio risk-return example.

lectures.title: Stanford EE364A Convex Optimization I Stephen Boyd I 2023 I Lecture 8
lectures.coverageNote: Lagrangian and dual problems, weak/strong duality, constraint qualifications, LP/QP duality, shadow prices, complementary slackness, KKT conditions, and sensitivity.

lectures.title: Stanford EE364A Convex Optimization I Stephen Boyd I 2023 I Lecture 9
lectures.coverageNote: Duality and reformulations; feasibility/alternatives; norm approximation, penalty functions, least-norm and regularized approximation, and robust approximation.

lectures.title: Stanford EE364A Convex Optimization I Stephen Boyd I 2023 I Lecture 10
lectures.coverageNote: Penalty/Huber functions, signal reconstruction and total-variation denoising, robust and regularized least squares, uncertainty, logistic regression, and hypothesis testing.

lectures.title: Stanford EE364A Convex Optimization I Stephen Boyd I 2023 I Lecture 11
lectures.coverageNote: Binary hypothesis testing and experiment design, followed by geometric optimization, minimum-volume and maximum-volume ellipsoids, approximation, and centering.

lectures.title: Stanford EE364A Convex Optimization I Stephen Boyd I 2023 I Lecture 12
lectures.coverageNote: Analytic centers and logarithmic barriers, ellipsoidal approximation, linear discrimination/separating hyperplanes, and robust classification formulations.

lectures.title: Stanford EE364A Convex Optimization I Stephen Boyd I 2023 I Lecture 13
lectures.coverageNote: Numerical linear algebra for optimization (Gaussian elimination, sparse LU/Cholesky, LDL, Schur complements and structure), then descent and gradient descent.

lectures.title: Stanford EE364A Convex Optimization I Stephen Boyd I 2023 I Lecture 14
lectures.coverageNote: Gradient-descent limitations and conditioning, steepest descent/norm choice, Newton's method and Newton decrement, convergence, damped/quadratic phases, practical behavior, and numerical linear algebra.

lectures.title: Stanford EE364A Convex Optimization I Stephen Boyd I 2023 I Lecture 15
lectures.coverageNote: Newton-method convergence/self-concordance and implementation, followed by interior-point/barrier-method concepts; pairs with Lectures 16–18 for the method sequence.

lectures.title: Stanford EE364A Convex Optimization I Stephen Boyd I 2023 I Lecture 16
lectures.coverageNote: Barrier function, central path, duality-gap certificates, KKT interpretation, barrier algorithm, convergence and phase-I methods.

lectures.title: Stanford EE364A Convex Optimization I Stephen Boyd I 2023 I Lecture 17
lectures.coverageNote: Barrier methods and solver implementation/performance; generalized inequalities, SDP/SOCP, cardinality relaxations, L1/sparse design, ML feature/classification examples, outliers and constraint violations.

lectures.title: Stanford EE364A Convex Optimization I Stephen Boyd I 2023 I Lecture 18
lectures.coverageNote: Course's final academic session continues sparse/cardinality modeling and L1-regularization examples, including piecewise-sparse formulations; viewing is a supplement to, not substitute for, the learner's audit assignment.

lectures.title: Lecture 22: Gradient Descent: Downhill to a Minimum
lectures.provider: MIT OpenCourseWare — 18.065 Matrix Methods in Data Analysis, Signal Processing, and Machine Learning
lectures.coverageNote: Focused MIT OCW substitute lesson explicitly about gradient descent for ML: first-derivative updates, ill-conditioned quadratic zig-zag behavior and convergence, plus least-squares gradient formulation. Official lecture page exposes its streamed/downloadable recording.

lectures.title: Lecture 23: Accelerating Gradient Descent (Use Momentum)
lectures.provider: MIT OpenCourseWare — 18.065 Matrix Methods in Data Analysis, Signal Processing, and Machine Learning
lectures.coverageNote: Full MIT OCW university lesson on momentum/heavy-ball and Nesterov acceleration; illustrates improved convergence on ill-conditioned quadratics and discusses mini-batch/stochastic gradient descent for large ML models. Not a full tutorial on modern adaptive optimizers or deep-network debugging.

unitMap.text: Weeks 1–2: convex sets/functions and modeling examples.
viewingSequence: L01 for motivation and examples of least squares, LP, and convex formulations.
L02 for convex sets, cones, polyhedra, inequalities, and set operations.
L03–L04 for convex functions, first/second-order characterization, Jensen, epigraphs, composition and perspective rules.
L05–L06 for recognizing valid convex optimization forms and modeling as LP/QP/QCQP/SOCP/GP.
coveredTopics: Convex and affine sets, convex hulls/cones, halfspaces, polyhedra, norm balls and the positive-semidefinite cone
Convex functions, first- and second-order conditions, Jensen's inequality, epigraphs, and composition/constructive rules
Recognizing/modeling standard convex problem forms and application examples
unitMap.practicalWork: Apply the recognition and modeling rules to original examples; passive viewing does not verify a learner's formulation.

unitMap.text: Weeks 3–4: least squares, LP/QP, Lagrange multipliers, and duality.
viewingSequence: L01 and L03 for least squares and quadratic objectives.
L05–L07 for optimization problem forms, LP/QP and SDP/portfolio examples.
L08 for Lagrangians, dual derivation, weak/strong duality, LP/QP examples, complementary slackness and KKT.
L09 for dual reformulations, feasibility/alternatives, norm approximation and regularization applications.
coveredTopics: Weak and strong duality, constraint qualifications, complementary slackness, KKT conditions, and sensitivity
unitMap.practicalWork: Derive the dual for the assigned learner-selected problem and check its assumptions; lectures supply theory, not a solution to that submission.

unitMap.text: Weeks 5–6: interior-point and first-order methods; CVXPY practice.
viewingSequence: L13 for numerical linear algebra and gradient descent foundations.
L14–L15 for conditioning, steepest descent, Newton updates/convergence, and self-concordance.
L16–L18 for barriers, central path, primal/dual certificates, phase I, interior-point implementation and performance.
S01–S02 as explicitly MIT OCW topic-matched supplements for conditioning, momentum, and Nesterov acceleration.
coveredTopics: Newton methods, conditioning, convergence behavior, and practical method tradeoffs
Barrier/interior-point methods, central path, duality-gap certificates, and feasibility/phase-I ideas
Numerical linear algebra underlying iterative optimization
uncoveredTopics: No verified video demonstrates CVXPY code/DCP syntax end-to-end, including problem construction, solver status, and residual checking; use the official Stanford text tutorial and perform the required coding practice.

Modern nonconvex neural-network training diagnostics and adaptive methods (for example, stochastic-noise effects and Adam-style optimizers) are not fully taught: MIT S02 only gives a focused momentum/Nesterov extension and brief mini-batch SGD context; no broader troubleshooting series was added.
unitMap.practicalWork: Use Stanford's official [CVXPY tutorial](https://www.cvxpy.org/tutorial/index.html) as written documentation, then implement and test the assigned CVXPY model yourself. The absence is specifically a video walkthrough, not an absence of public documentation or of optimization-method video coverage.

unitMap.text: Weeks 7–8: regularization, sparse recovery, robust objectives, and ML applications.
viewingSequence: L07 for portfolio risk/return and multicriterion tradeoffs.
L09–L10 for norm/penalty approximation, robust least squares, regularization, signal recovery and ML examples.
L11–L12 for convex experiment design/geometric modeling and linear-discrimination formulations.
L17–L18 for cardinality relaxations, L1 sparsity, selection/classification, and sparse design examples.
coveredTopics: Regularized and norm-penalized least squares; Huber/penalty objectives
Robust approximation, uncertainty modeling, and total-variation/signal reconstruction examples
Cardinality relaxation, L1 sparsity, sparse design/recovery and ML feature selection
Logistic regression, hypothesis testing, linear discrimination/classification, portfolio tradeoffs, and related application examples
unitMap.practicalWork: Examples help choose and interpret models but do not establish that a learner has validated a particular dataset, allocation, or model.

unitMap.text: Weeks 9–10: optimization audit of a training or allocation problem.
viewingSequence: L01 and L07 for application framing, engineering examples, and portfolio allocation tradeoffs.
L08–L10 for dual/KKT/sensitivity reasoning and robust/regularized ML objectives.
L13–L18 for solver, conditioning, numerical method, barrier and sparse-model diagnostics useful when auditing a formulation.
coveredTopics: Problem formulation and application tradeoffs for ML and allocation examples
Dual/KKT/sensitivity concepts relevant to solution validation
Conditioning, numerical method choice and solver-performance caveats
unitMap.practicalWork: The optimization audit is original learner work. The assignment remains: formulate and solve a constrained ML/CSE design problem in CVXPY; derive its dual, validate KKT residuals, and compare a first-order solver with a closed-form or baseline method. Videos do not perform the audit or its evidence gathering.

remainingGaps: CVXPY-specific video practice remains uncovered: no verified public lecture in the selected sources walks through CVXPY/DCP code, solver status, and residual checks. Stanford's official CVXPY tutorial is public text documentation; the learner still must implement and validate the model.

Modern nonconvex/deep-network optimizer failure modes remain only partly covered. The primary Stanford sequence covers convex gradient/steepest descent, Newton methods, conditioning, logistic/classification examples and solver tradeoffs; MIT OCW Lecture 23 adds momentum/Nesterov and mentions mini-batch SGD but is not a comprehensive SGD/Adam training-diagnostics lecture.

Unit 3: No verified video demonstrates CVXPY code/DCP syntax end-to-end, including problem construction, solver status, and residual checking; use the official Stanford text tutorial and perform the required coding practice.

Unit 3: Modern nonconvex neural-network training diagnostics and adaptive methods (for example, stochastic-noise effects and Adam-style optimizers) are not fully taught: MIT S02 only gives a focused momentum/Nesterov extension and brief mini-batch SGD context; no broader troubleshooting series was added.

courses.title: Numerical Methods and Numerical Linear Algebra
courses.level: Graduate numerical-methods video foundation; MIT 18.335J readings extend numerical linear algebra and error analysis.
courses.prerequisites: AI-B02 and AI-G04; programming fluency and calculus.
objectives: Analyze floating-point error, conditioning, stability, and backward error.
Choose dense/sparse direct and iterative solvers for linear systems and eigenproblems.
Implement interpolation, integration, root-finding, and nonlinear optimization with diagnostics.
Distinguish mathematical accuracy from numerical reliability in ML and simulation pipelines.
units: Weeks 1–2: machine arithmetic, error propagation, conditioning, and stability.
Weeks 3–4: dense/sparse factorizations, Krylov methods, and eigenproblems.
Weeks 5–6: interpolation, quadrature, nonlinear equations, and differentiation.
Weeks 7–8: numerical optimization and adjoint sensitivities.
Weeks 9–10: replicate a numerical failure, repair it, and document tolerances/tests.
courses.assignment: Reproduce a numerically unstable computation, demonstrate the failure empirically, implement a stable alternative, and write an error/conditioning report with automated regression tests.
courses.assessment: Rubric: analysis of error/stability 35%; experimental design 25%; stable implementation/tests 25%; communication of numerical limits 15%. Pass threshold: 70%.
courses.mapping: Harvard outcomes 2, 6, 7, and 9: assess numerical approaches, efficiency and error; build reliable simulations and analyses.

unitMap.text: Weeks 1–2: machine arithmetic, error propagation, conditioning, and stability.
viewingSequence: Start with MIT18S096-L3P2 for finite-difference approximation/error context.
Use LAMAR-NA-ROOTERR and LAMAR-NA-DIFF for observed root-iteration and difference-quotient errors/cancellation/truncation.
Finish with M086-L02, M086-L03, M086-L24 for consistency, accuracy, stability and error-estimate context.
coveredTopics: Examples of iterative root-finding error, convergence behavior, and catastrophic cancellation
Discretization accuracy, stability, convergence and error estimates for numerical methods
uncoveredTopics: Floating-point representation/IEEE rounding and roundoff propagation
Conditioning and forward-versus-backward error as separate general numerical-analysis concepts; MIT 18.335J course materials discuss these, but its OCW index exposes no course lecture recordings.
unitMap.practicalWork: Use the assignment experiment to quantify error empirically; viewings do not provide a measured result for the learner’s chosen computation.

unitMap.text: Weeks 3–4: dense/sparse factorizations, Krylov methods, and eigenproblems.
viewingSequence: Begin with MIT18-06-L04 for dense LU factorization; then M086-L12 and M086-L13 for matrix structure and reordered sparse elimination.
Watch M086-L15, M086-L16, M086-L17, M086-L18 and M086-L19 in order for iterative/preconditioned sparse methods, multigrid, Krylov methods and conjugate gradients.
For eigenproblems, use MIT18-06-L21 and MIT18-06-L25, then MIT18-06-L29 and MIT18-06-L33 for SVD/pseudoinverse foundations; MIT18S096-L8P1 adds eigenproblem sensitivity (not eigensolving).
coveredTopics: Preconditioned iterative methods, multigrid, Krylov methods and conjugate gradients
Eigenvalues/eigenvectors, symmetric positive-definite matrices, SVD and pseudoinverse foundations
uncoveredTopics: Numerical eigenvalue/eigenvector algorithms and solver-selection tradeoffs (e.g., explicit iterative eigensolvers) are not taught by these linear-algebra and eigen-sensitivity recordings.
unitMap.practicalWork: Learner must still select, implement, benchmark and justify a solver for the assigned data/problem; recordings are not solver tests.

unitMap.text: Weeks 5–6: interpolation, quadrature, nonlinear equations, and differentiation.
viewingSequence: Watch LAMAR-NA-ROOT then LAMAR-NA-ROOTERR for bisection/Newton and error/convergence.
For differentiation, watch MIT18S096-L3P2 followed by LAMAR-NA-DIFF (difference-quotient errors).
For quadrature, view LAMAR-NA-QUAD1, LAMAR-NA-QUAD2 and LAMAR-NA-QUAD3 in sequence; QUAD2 explicitly derives a quadrature rule using polynomial interpolation.
Finish with MIT18S096-L4P2 for a university lecture connecting nonlinear root finding and optimization.
coveredTopics: Bisection and Newton root finding, error/convergence examples
Composite Newton–Cotes/Simpson-type and Gaussian quadrature; quadrature derivation from interpolating polynomials
uncoveredTopics: General-purpose polynomial/spline interpolation choices, interpolation error bounds and stability beyond the polynomial-interpolation step inside a quadrature derivation.
unitMap.practicalWork: The assignment’s algorithms still require learner implementation and diagnostics; no video substitutes for the coding.

unitMap.text: Weeks 7–8: numerical optimization and adjoint sensitivities.
viewingSequence: Start with M086-L21 and M086-L22 for constrained optimization and weighted least squares.
View M086-L23 through M086-L29 in order for variational formulation, error/projection, constraint, regularization, duality and inverse-problem perspectives.
Use MIT18-06-L16 and MIT18-06-L27 for least-squares and positive-definite minima foundations.
Complete MIT18S096-L4P2 then MIT18S096-L6P1 for optimization/adjoint gradients and adjoint sensitivities of ODE solutions.
coveredTopics: Constrained optimization, weighted least squares, regularization, duality and inverse problems
unitMap.practicalWork: The learner must implement the chosen optimization/sensitivity method and assess diagnostics in their own pipeline.

unitMap.text: Weeks 9–10: replicate a numerical failure, repair it, and document tolerances/tests.
viewingSequence: Review M086-L02 and M086-L03 for stability/accuracy concepts, with M086-L24 for error estimates.
Use LAMAR-NA-ROOTERR, LAMAR-NA-DIFF and MIT18S096-L3P2 as examples of measured algorithmic error and approximation behavior.
Apply these ideas to the learner’s own failure and regression-test record; the videos are background, not project evidence.
coveredTopics: Accuracy/stability and error-estimate concepts for interpreting numerical failures
uncoveredTopics: The Unit 1 floating-point/conditioning/backward-error video gap carries into failure diagnosis; automated regression-test design is not a taught video topic and must be performed in the project.
unitMap.practicalWork: The entire capstone assignment is learner work: reproduce a numerically unstable computation, demonstrate it empirically, implement a stable alternative, write the error/conditioning report and create automated regression tests. Video viewing cannot substitute for any deliverable.

remainingGaps: Weeks 1–2: No verified free lecture recording located for IEEE floating-point representation/roundoff propagation and the general conditioning/forward-versus-backward-error framework. MIT 18.335J offers notes/readings but no lecture videos on its OCW resource inventory; closest videos cover discretization error, stability, root-method error and cancellation.

Weeks 3–4: No verified public video lecture located teaching numerical eigensolver algorithms and comparative solver selection; available videos cover eigen foundations and eigenproblem sensitivities, not algorithms such as numerical iterative eigensolvers.

Weeks 5–6: Verified video coverage includes interpolation as used to derive a quadrature rule, but no verified lecture located covering general polynomial/spline interpolation method selection, stability and error bounds.

Unit 1: Conditioning and forward-versus-backward error as separate general numerical-analysis concepts; MIT 18.335J course materials discuss these, but its OCW index exposes no course lecture recordings.
Unit 2: Numerical eigenvalue/eigenvector algorithms and solver-selection tradeoffs (e.g., explicit iterative eigensolvers) are not taught by these linear-algebra and eigen-sensitivity recordings.
Unit 3: General-purpose polynomial/spline interpolation choices, interpolation error bounds and stability beyond the polynomial-interpolation step inside a quadrature derivation.

Unit 5: The Unit 1 floating-point/conditioning/backward-error video gap carries into failure diagnosis; automated regression-test design is not a taught video topic and must be performed in the project.

courses.title: Scientific Machine Learning, Simulation, and Parallel Computing
courses.level: Graduate core / CSE concentration
courses.prerequisites: AI-G04 and AI-G05. Julia is recommended; Python learners may use equivalent tools only when they can benchmark them.
objectives: Build differentiable programs for dynamical systems and inverse problems.
Use automatic differentiation and adjoints to estimate parameters or control simulations.
Profile and parallelize serial, threaded, distributed, or GPU workloads.
Compare data-driven and mechanistic models with appropriate error and performance measures.
Produce a reproducible scientific-computing artifact with a credible performance claim.
units: Weeks 1–2: Julia/numerical performance, automatic differentiation, and matrix calculus.
Weeks 3–4: ODEs/PDEs, neural differential equations, PINNs, and adjoints.
Weeks 5–6: serial profiling, memory, threads, and GPU parallelism.
Weeks 7–8: distributed/MPI methods and performance measurement.
Weeks 9–12: scientific ML project, reproducibility package, and presentation.
courses.assignment: Create a SciML model for a documented physical or social dynamical system. Compare a mechanistic baseline with a differentiable/learned component, profile it, and deliver a reproducible benchmark.
courses.assessment: Rubric: model/assumption quality 25%; numerical/AD correctness 25%; performance methodology 20%; reproducibility/documentation 20%; scientific interpretation 10%. Pass threshold: 70%.
courses.mapping: Harvard outcomes 1–3, 6–10, especially simulation, reproducible analysis, parallel/distributed computing, maintainable software, and domain breakthroughs.

objectives: Implement tokenization, embeddings, sequence models, attention, and transformer fine-tuning.

courses.title: Reinforcement Learning, Control, and Sequential Decision-Making
courses.level: Graduate core
courses.prerequisites: AI-G01, AI-G03, AI-G04, and AI-G07; probability, optimization, and strong Python required.
objectives: Formulate a decision problem as an MDP/POMDP with state, action, dynamics, reward, and safety constraints.
Derive and implement value-based, policy-gradient, actor-critic, and model-based algorithms.
Explain distribution shift, offline RL, imitation learning, exploration, and RL-from-feedback risks.
Evaluate policies with uncertainty, reproducible seeds, and appropriate baselines.
units: Weeks 1–2: imitation learning, MDPs, dynamic programming, and policy evaluation.
Weeks 3–4: policy gradients, actor-critic, Q-learning, and replay.
Weeks 5–6: model-based RL, variational/control-as-inference, and offline RL.
Weeks 7–8: exploration, multi-task RL, LLM RL/RLHF, and theory.
Weeks 9–12: safe simulator experiment, ablation, and policy-evaluation report.
courses.assignment: Use a simulator—not a real-world high-stakes environment—to compare an offline or online RL method with a behavior-cloning/value baseline. Report seeds, uncertainty, reward-hacking cases, and a safety constraint.
courses.assessment: Rubric: MDP/problem specification 20%; correct algorithm 25%; evaluation/reproducibility 25%; safety/reward analysis 20%; clear reporting 10%. Pass threshold: 70%.

unitMap.text: Weeks 1–2: imitation learning, MDPs, dynamic programming, and policy evaluation.
viewingSequence: Start with Berkeley Lecture 2, Parts 1–5 for imitation learning / behavioral cloning and the distribution-shift motivation.
Watch Berkeley Lecture 4, Parts 1–6 for RL/MDP foundations, then Stanford CS234 Lecture 1 for an explicit MDP modeling exercise.
Watch Stanford CS234 Lecture 2 for tabular MDP planning/dynamic programming, then Lecture 3 for policy evaluation. Berkeley Lecture 1, Parts 1–3 are optional course framing.
coveredTopics: State, action, transition, reward, and sequential decision formulation for MDPs
Tabular MDP planning and dynamic programming
uncoveredTopics: POMDP observation and belief-state formulation (course objective, not named in the unit text): selected verified recordings establish MDPs but do not teach this full topic.
unitMap.practicalWork: Watching does not replace implementing the imitation-learning/MDP exercises. No enrollment, credit, certificate, or credential is conferred.

unitMap.text: Weeks 3–4: policy gradients, actor-critic, Q-learning, and replay.
viewingSequence: Watch Berkeley Lecture 5, Parts 1–6 on policy gradients.
Continue with Lecture 6, Parts 1–5 on actor-critic; then Lecture 7, Parts 1–4 on value-function methods.
Finish with Lecture 8, Parts 1–6 on Q-functions/Q-learning and replay-based deep RL.
unitMap.practicalWork: Apply these lectures by implementing and debugging the assigned algorithms; videos do not substitute for code or assessed work.

unitMap.text: Weeks 5–6: model-based RL, variational/control-as-inference, and offline RL.
viewingSequence: For planning/control and dynamics models, watch Berkeley Lecture 10, Parts 1–5, then Lectures 11 and 12 in playlist-part order.
Watch Lecture 18, Parts 1–4 on variational inference before Lecture 19, Parts 1–5 on control as inference.
Complete with Lectures 15 and 16 in part order for offline RL.
coveredTopics: Model-based RL and model-based policy learning
Variational inference and generative models in RL
unitMap.practicalWork: Implement/compare an offline or online method as assigned; viewing is not a substitute for the simulator work.

unitMap.text: Weeks 7–8: exploration, multi-task RL, LLM RL/RLHF, and theory.
viewingSequence: Watch Berkeley Lecture 13, Parts 1–6, then Lecture 14, Parts 1–4 for exploration.
Watch Lecture 17, Parts 1–2 for RL theory; the statistical-foundations guest lecture (b23-087) is a deeper optional theory supplement.
Watch Lecture 20, Parts 1–4 on inverse RL as a bridge to reward inference; then Eric Mitchell’s full RLHF algorithms/applications guest lecture (b23-086).
Finish with Lecture 21, Parts 1–3 on sequence/language models and Lecture 22, Parts 1–5 on transfer and multi-task/meta-learning.
coveredTopics: RL from human feedback (RLHF) algorithms and applications
unitMap.practicalWork: The recorded lectures support the theoretical topics but do not certify expertise or replace assignments. The RLHF guest lecture is an academic course recording, not an enrollment-only service.

unitMap.text: Weeks 9–12: safe simulator experiment, ablation, and policy-evaluation report.
viewingSequence: Choose an appropriate comparison and behavior-cloning baseline from Berkeley Lecture 2, Parts 1–5; review an online value-based baseline in Lecture 8, Parts 1–6, or an offline method in Lectures 15–16.
Review Berkeley Lecture 17 for algorithmic/theoretical evaluation considerations and Stanford CS234 Lecture 3 for policy evaluation under sampled outcomes.
Use Berkeley Lecture 23, Parts 1–2 for challenges/open problems and Berkeley Lecture 4 for reward/objective framing; then conduct the simulator experiment and write the report yourself.
coveredTopics: Candidate offline/online RL methods and behavior-cloning baseline
Comparative experimental framing and open challenges
uncoveredTopics: A full treatment of constrained/safe RL algorithms and formal safety-constraint design for the simulator is not established by the selected lectures; the intro/reward-hacking and challenges content is only partial coverage.
A dedicated lecture on multi-seed uncertainty estimation, ablation methodology, and reproducibility/reporting practice is not verified in the inventory.
unitMap.practicalWork: Learner must implement a simulator experiment (never a high-stakes real-world deployment), baseline, ablation, repeated-seed/uncertainty analysis, reward-hacking review, safety constraint, and report. Video viewing cannot perform this fieldwork or substitute for the original assignment and rubric.

remainingGaps: POMDP observation and belief-state formulation (course objective): MDP framing and tabular planning have verified public-video coverage, but no selected lecture fully covers POMDP modeling.

Formal safe/constrained RL methods and safety-constraint design: the selected introductory reward-hacking/challenges material is partial, not a complete lecture on safety-constrained policy optimization.

A dedicated lesson on multi-seed uncertainty estimation, ablation methodology, and reproducible evaluation reporting was not verified; apply these requirements through learner work, not by inferring video coverage.

courses.title: AI Systems: Distributed, Reliable, and Efficient ML Infrastructure
courses.level: Graduate core
courses.prerequisites: AI-G02 and AI-G07; strong programming. MIT 6.5840 expects systems background, so complete the listed systems readings/labs before advanced extensions.
objectives: Explain RPC, concurrency, replication, consistency, fault tolerance, and sharding.
Implement and test a distributed service with explicit failure assumptions.
Connect systems tradeoffs to ML data pipelines, training, inference, observability, and cost.
Measure throughput, tail latency, consistency/failure behavior, and reproducibility.
Identify the gap between the distributed-systems base course and specialized accelerator/MLOps content.
units: Weeks 1–2: threads, RPC, map-reduce, and failure models.
Weeks 3–4: replication, primary-backup, consensus, and Raft.
Weeks 5–6: sharding, transactions/consistency, and load/performance.
Weeks 7–8: connect systems patterns to data lineage, model serving, and evaluation.
Weeks 9–12: build a fault-injected service; write an ML-systems design review.
courses.assignment: Complete a bounded distributed key-value/service lab or equivalent and extend it with a model-serving or experiment-tracking interface. Run failure injection and publish latency/consistency results plus an architecture decision record.
courses.assessment: Rubric: systems correctness/tests 30%; failure model and experiments 25%; performance/observability 20%; AI-systems gap analysis 15%; documentation 10%. Pass threshold: 70%.
courses.mapping: Harvard outcomes 2–3, 6, 8–9: choose efficient infrastructure, use parallel/distributed computing, and build robust, maintainable artifacts.

lectures.title: Lecture 11: Cache Consistency: Frangipani
lectures.coverageNote: Distributed cache consistency.

lectures.title: Lecture 12: Distributed Transactions

lectures.title: Lecture 13: Spanner

lectures.title: Lecture 14: Optimistic Concurrency Control

lectures.coverageNote: Peer-to-peer distributed protocol case study.

lectures.title: Lecture 20: Blockstack
lectures.coverageNote: Distributed naming/storage system case study.

unitMap.text: Weeks 1–2: threads, RPC, map-reduce, and failure models.
viewingSequence: 1. Watch Lecture 1 for distributed-system goals, failure assumptions, and MapReduce framing.
2. Watch Lecture 2 for RPC and threads.
3. Watch Lecture 15 for the Spark/MapReduce processing model.
unitMap.practicalWork: Complete video coverage for the listed academic concepts; implement/test the concepts in the course lab independently.

unitMap.text: Weeks 3–4: replication, primary-backup, consensus, and Raft.
viewingSequence: 1. Watch Lecture 4 for primary-backup.
2. Watch Lectures 5–7 for Raft and fault tolerance.
3. Watch Lectures 8–10 for coordination and replication case studies.
unitMap.practicalWork: Videos teach concepts; implement and test the replicated service yourself.

unitMap.text: Weeks 5–6: sharding, transactions/consistency, and load/performance.
viewingSequence: 1. Watch Lecture 3 for GFS data distribution.
2. Watch Lectures 10–11 and 16–17 for replication and consistency tradeoffs.
3. Watch Lectures 12–14 for transactions, Spanner, and optimistic concurrency.
uncoveredTopics: explicit shard/key partitioning, shard ownership and movement/rebalancing, and end-to-end sharded-service behavior are assigned in the lab but not taught by a verified direct lecture in the primary public video series.
unitMap.practicalWork: MIT 6.824’s official schedule assigns a Sharded KV lab but exposes no corresponding public lecture video; the covered cases do not substitute for explicit sharding mechanics. The learner must implement the sharded lab and measure load/performance.

unitMap.text: Weeks 7–8: connect systems patterns to data lineage, model serving, and evaluation.
viewingSequence: 1. Watch MIT 6.824 Lecture 15 for distributed processing foundations.
2. Watch MIT 6.5940 Lectures 19–20 for ML distributed training.
3. Watch MIT 6.5940 Lecture 13 for efficient inference/serving.
4. Watch the Stanford MLSys seminar for production objectives, metrics tradeoffs, and changing data context.
coveredTopics: distributed data-processing foundation for ML pipelines (Spark)
distributed training parallelism and communication/performance bottlenecks
production latency-throughput tradeoffs and changing data context
uncoveredTopics: ML-specific data lineage/feature tracking; model-quality evaluation and feedback; drift/monitoring and observability practice are not fully covered by these videos.
unitMap.practicalWork: The lectures provide foundations, not an operational lineage/monitoring stack. Add instrumentation, evaluation, and reproducibility evidence in your own design review.

unitMap.text: Weeks 9–12: build a fault-injected service; write an ML-systems design review.
viewingSequence: 1. Revisit Lectures 1, 4, and 6–7 to define assumptions and failure cases.
2. Use Lectures 10 and 12 to compare database/transaction design tradeoffs.
3. Watch MIT 6.5940 Lectures 19–20 and 13 for ML training/serving constraints.
4. Use the Stanford seminar as a design-context supplement, then write and test your own review.
coveredTopics: distributed training/serving tradeoffs relevant to architecture review
uncoveredTopics: hands-on service implementation and failure injection; empirical throughput/tail-latency/consistency/reproducibility results; and the written ML-systems design review/architecture decision record remain learner-authored work; videos do not provide a complete course-specific review method.
unitMap.practicalWork: Videos cannot substitute for the assignment: complete a bounded distributed key-value/service lab or equivalent, extend it with model serving or experiment tracking, run failure injection, publish latency/consistency results and an architecture decision record. Submit your own ML-systems design review.

remainingGaps: Explicit sharding/partition ownership, shard movement or rebalancing, and sharded-service operation: the official MIT archive links a Sharded KV lab, but no verified individual public lecture for the lab was found. GFS/Spanner are partial conceptual context, not complete coverage.

ML-specific lineage and feature tracking, model-quality evaluation/feedback, drift monitoring, and production observability: Spark and the Stanford seminar offer useful partial foundations, but no verified free recording found in the bounded targeted search fully teaches this set.

Course-specific design-review/ADR method and empirical capstone execution (fault injection; throughput, tail latency, consistency, and reproducibility measurements) remain learner work; available lectures provide background, not completion.

Unit 3: explicit shard/key partitioning, shard ownership and movement/rebalancing, and end-to-end sharded-service behavior are assigned in the lab but not taught by a verified direct lecture in the primary public video series.
Unit 4: ML-specific data lineage/feature tracking; model-quality evaluation and feedback; drift/monitoring and observability practice are not fully covered by these videos.

Unit 5: hands-on service implementation and failure injection; empirical throughput/tail-latency/consistency/reproducibility results; and the written ML-systems design review/architecture decision record remain learner-authored work; videos do not provide a complete course-specific review method.

courses.title: Responsible AI, Fairness, Safety, and Governance
courses.level: Graduate core integrative requirement
courses.prerequisites: AI-G01 and AI-G03; take after at least one generative-AI or deployed-system course. It is not a substitute for legal, regulatory, or domain-expert advice.
objectives: Distinguish statistical fairness criteria, causal questions, and their incompatibilities or limits.
Audit datasets, model outcomes, and deployment processes for bias, calibration, privacy, and misuse risks.
Evaluate LLM/GenAI risks including fabricated content, data provenance, prompt injection, harmful outputs, and over-reliance.
Design monitoring, human oversight, documentation, incident response, and governance controls.
Communicate evidence, uncertainty, and tradeoffs to technical and nontechnical stakeholders.
units: Weeks 1–2: legitimacy, protected attributes, fairness definitions, and impossibility/tradeoff cases.
Weeks 3–4: causal reasoning, datasets, measurement, and evaluation design.
Weeks 5–6: generative-AI safety, privacy, provenance, and adversarial misuse.
Weeks 7–8: governance, model cards, impact assessments, monitoring, and incident response.
Weeks 9–10: independent audit and a board-ready risk memo.
courses.assignment: Conduct an end-to-end responsible-AI review of a prior track project: data sheet, subgroup/calibration analysis where appropriate, red-team scenarios, model/system card, deployment controls, and a 4-page governance memo.
courses.assessment: Rubric: problem framing/stakeholders 20%; technical audit 25%; evidence and limitations 20%; controls/monitoring 20%; clear cross-disciplinary communication 15%. Pass threshold: 70%.
courses.mapping: Harvard outcomes 1–4, 6–7, 9–10: frame real-world problems, communicate across disciplines, model data responsibly, and build accountable artifacts.

courses.title: Financial Reporting & Control
courses.level: MBA core mapping; the primary NPTEL series is an external IIT undergraduate/professional substitute, not HBS graduate credit.
courses.prerequisites: Comfort with percentages and algebra; complete the diagnostic in Unit 1.
objectives: Construct and connect income statement, balance sheet, and cash-flow statement.
Interpret revenue, inventory, depreciation, working-capital, and cash-flow choices.
Use ratios and common-size analysis to form a lender/investor view.
Identify governance, reporting-quality, and control risks in a public filing.
units: Unit 1: Watch lectures 1–5; map the accounting equation and rebuild a simple balance sheet.
Unit 2: Watch lectures 6–15; post revenue, depreciation, inventory, and cash-flow adjustments in a spreadsheet.
Unit 3: Watch lectures 16–24; compare standards, governance models, and control failures.
Unit 4: Watch lectures 25–35; complete one of the posted statement-analysis cases and calculate ratios.
Unit 5: Watch lectures 36–40; write and revise an investor-oriented quality-of-earnings memo.
courses.assignment: Analyze two consecutive annual reports for one listed company; submit a three-statement linkage model, 12 ratios, five adjustments/risks, and a 1,200-word credit or investment memo.
courses.assessment: Rubric (100%): accurate statements and reconciliations 35; economic interpretation 30; controls/governance diagnosis 20; source discipline and clarity 15.
courses.mapping: HBS Required Curriculum: Financial Reporting & Control (FRC).
