unitMap.text: Unit 1: Watch lectures 1–5; map the accounting equation and rebuild a simple balance sheet.
viewingSequence: MBA101-P01 then P02: accounting scope and statements.
MBA101-P03 through P07: balance-sheet sequence; construct and reconcile the learner balance sheet.
coveredTopics: purpose and scope of financial accounting
financial statements and their relationship to the accounting equation
rebuilding a simple balance sheet from accounting information
unitMap.practicalWork: The diagnostic and spreadsheet/balance-sheet reconstruction remain learner work; viewing does not complete them.

unitMap.text: Unit 2: Watch lectures 6–15; post revenue, depreciation, inventory, and cash-flow adjustments in a spreadsheet.
viewingSequence: MBA101-P06 through P07: balance-sheet sequence.
MBA101-P08 through P10: income statement and revenue context.
MBA101-P11 through P13: depreciation and inventory valuation.
MBA101-P14 through P15: begin cash-flow mechanics; P16-P18 are in the next original unit range and can be watched as a continuation if the working-capital bridge remains unclear.
coveredTopics: cash-flow statement foundations and adjustments in the assigned lectures
uncoveredTopics: A clearly indexed, complete working-capital reconciliation (for example, receivables, inventory and payables changes into operating cash flow) is not verified in the titles/index for Unit 2 lectures 6–15; the five-part cash-flow sequence continues beyond this assigned range.
unitMap.practicalWork: Posting transactions and cash-flow adjustments in a spreadsheet is required learner work; videos do not create or validate the spreadsheet.

unitMap.text: Unit 3: Watch lectures 16–24; compare standards, governance models, and control failures.
viewingSequence: MBA101-P16 through P18: finish the primary cash-flow-statement sequence assigned at the start of this unit.
MBA101-P19 through P21: governance, global governance models and the Enron case.
MBA101-P22 through P24: standards/principles, accounting evolution and recording transactions.
MBA101-S59 then S60: supplemental reporting regulation and standards, including IFRS convergence and US GAAP differences.
coveredTopics: cash-flow statement construction and interpretation (continuation of primary sequence)
corporate governance concepts and global governance models
cross-framework standards differences and comparability at a conceptual level (supplemental lecture)
financial reporting regulation and disclosure context
uncoveredTopics: A detailed internal-control-over-financial-reporting framework, control-testing procedure or control-risk assessment method is not directly indexed in the selected public lectures; Enron is a governance-failure case, not a substitute for that applied control work.
unitMap.practicalWork: Comparing current accounting standards against a public filing and diagnosing control risks require independent filing research. The IIT Roorkee supplement is an explicitly labeled external university substitute, not HBS credit; its India-specific discussion is older and should not be treated as current legal/accounting guidance.

unitMap.text: Unit 4: Watch lectures 25–35; complete one of the posted statement-analysis cases and calculate ratios.
viewingSequence: MBA101-P25 through P28: follow statement case work across income statement, balance sheet and cash flow.
MBA101-P29 through P31: statement interpretation and ratio analysis.
MBA101-P32 through P35: worked Shipping Corporation of India analysis case.
MBA101-S34: optional second-university explanation of financial-statement analysis and ratio interpretation.
uncoveredTopics: Explicit common-size (vertical percentage) statement analysis is not identified in the verified primary lecture titles; supplemental lecture 34 addresses statement analysis and ratios but its checked title/chapter index does not establish common-size coverage.
unitMap.practicalWork: Completing the posted case and calculating the required ratios remain learner work; the videos are instruction, not case answers or grading.

unitMap.text: Unit 5: Watch lectures 36–40; write and revise an investor-oriented quality-of-earnings memo.
viewingSequence: MBA101-P36 then P37: analyze the TCS case.
MBA101-P38 then P39: analyze the RIL case.
MBA101-P40: review the primary course, then write and revise the investor-oriented memo.
coveredTopics: applied analysis of public-company financial statements through TCS and RIL cases
uncoveredTopics: A systematic quality-of-earnings method (recurring versus nonrecurring earnings, accrual quality, earnings persistence, and earnings-management red flags) is not explicit in the verified primary lecture index. Cases give applied analysis but do not establish full topic coverage.
unitMap.practicalWork: The two-year annual-report comparison, three-statement linkage model, 12 ratios, five adjustments/risks, and 1,200-word credit/investment memo—and its revision—remain learner work; videos cannot substitute for this capstone.

courses.title: Finance I: Valuation, Risk, and Capital Allocation
courses.level: MBA core mapping; MIT 15.401 is a graduate Sloan course and the closest open primary substitute.
courses.prerequisites: MBA-101 recommended; algebra, spreadsheet fluency, and present-value basics required.
objectives: Value cash flows using discounting, bonds, equities, and no-arbitrage logic.
Estimate risk, expected return, and portfolio trade-offs.
Apply CAPM/APT intuition to a capital-budgeting recommendation.
Explain when market efficiency and derivatives matter to a managerial decision.
units: Unit 1: Watch introduction and present-value sections; build a discounting and bond-pricing workbook.
Unit 2: Watch fixed-income and equities sections; estimate prices and yields from a small data set.
Unit 3: Watch forwards, futures, options, and risk/return sections; diagram payoffs and hedge one exposure.
Unit 4: Watch portfolio and CAPM/APT sections; compare portfolios and explain assumptions.
Unit 5: Watch capital budgeting, efficiency, and summary sections; prepare the investment committee case.
courses.assignment: Prepare an investment-committee deck for a $10m project: forecast free cash flow, choose discount rate, calculate NPV/IRR, run sensitivity analysis, and state a hedge/financing recommendation.
courses.assessment: Rubric (100%): model integrity 35; valuation and risk reasoning 30; assumptions/sensitivity 20; decision communication 15.

lectures.title: Marketing Metrics
lectures.provider: NPTEL / IIT Kanpur (Business Marketing – Technology Focus; Prof. Jayanta Chatterjee)
lectures.coverageNote: Full public NPTEL academic lesson; transcript/player checked. Explains marketing dashboard design and metrics including new-customer acquisition, retention, market share, product development, sales, margins/profitability, break-even, customer awareness/attitude, trials, social/digital engagement, forecasts and budgets. Business-to-business examples; transfer thoughtfully to the learner launch.

unitMap.text: Unit 1: Watch lectures 1–12; create a category map and a PESTEL/competitor scan.
viewingSequence: Watch primary-series lectures 1–12 in order.
coveredTopics: Marketing definition, core concepts, services, historical evolution and contemporary practice
Marketing objectives, planning/strategy and core competencies
unitMap.practicalWork: Create the assigned category map and conduct a real category PESTEL/competitor scan; videos supply methods, not current market evidence.

unitMap.text: Unit 2: Watch lectures 13–24; draft a research instrument and sampling plan.
viewingSequence: Watch primary-series lectures 13–24 in order.
coveredTopics: Marketing research process and the distinction between MDP and MRP
Data collection, preparation, analysis and multivariate analysis
unitMap.practicalWork: Draft and pilot a research instrument and justify the sampling plan; viewing is not a substitute for designing or testing the instrument.

unitMap.text: Unit 3: Watch lectures 25–36; interview five prospective users and synthesize a buyer journey.
viewingSequence: Watch primary-series lectures 25–36 in order.
coveredTopics: Consumer need recognition, information search, evaluation, purchase and post-purchase behavior
Socio-cultural and psychological influences and consumer attitudes
Industrial buying behavior, organizational buying processes and industrial marketing
Buyer-process dimensions and related managerial implications
unitMap.practicalWork: Interview five prospective users as prescribed by the course and synthesize their actual evidence into a buyer journey; videos cannot perform fieldwork.

unitMap.text: Unit 4: Watch lectures 37–48; select a segment, target, positioning, and brand promise.
viewingSequence: Watch primary-series lectures 37–46 in order.
Then watch supplement MBA103-MMII-018 for measurement of brand equity and related constructs.
The official course page lists lectures 47–48 but their individual public playback links were not exposed in the checked index; do not infer their content from the repeated generic title.
coveredTopics: Segmentation bases, segment selection and targeting, including B2B
Branding, differentiation and crafting a brand promise
uncoveredTopics: The official NPTEL page names lectures 47 and 48 “Generic Modeling Strategy”; their individual recordings/direct playback links could not be verified, so that named content remains a video gap.
unitMap.practicalWork: The learner must select and substantiate the segment and target and write a positioning statement/brand promise; neither video viewing nor the equity supplement makes those decisions.

unitMap.text: Unit 5: Price, channel-test, and present a one-page launch dashboard with metrics.
viewingSequence: Watch Marketing Management II lectures 25–30 in order (pricing).
Watch Marketing Management II lectures 31–34 in order (distribution and channels).
Finish with the standalone NPTEL “Marketing Metrics” academic lesson.
coveredTopics: Pricing considerations, demand and cost estimation, break-even and alternative pricing methods
Distribution, channel forms/dynamics/options and integrated channel design
Marketing dashboard logic and measures for acquisition, retention, share, sales, product performance, profitability/margins, break-even, trials and marketing communication
unitMap.practicalWork: Actually price the offer, run or design the channel test, select defensible launch measures and present the one-page 90-day dashboard. The metrics substitute is an IIT Kanpur B2B lesson; adapt its general dashboard principles and examples critically to the chosen market.

remainingGaps: MBA-103 Unit 4: Public NPTEL course page lists primary lectures 47–48 as “Generic Modeling Strategy”, but the checked public per-lecture index exposes only lectures 1–46 and the corresponding 47/48 media endpoints were unavailable (404). No direct entries are fabricated; the named generic-modeling-strategy lesson content remains uncovered.

courses.title: Technology & Operations Management
courses.level: MBA core mapping; NPTEL/IIT production-and-operations series is an external professional substitute.
courses.prerequisites: Basic algebra and spreadsheet skills; MBA-101 and MBA-103 helpful.
objectives: Map processes and quantify capacity, bottlenecks, flow time, and utilization.
Use forecasting, inventory, quality, and scheduling tools in operations choices.
Link process design and supply-chain choices to competitive strategy.
Design a practical improvement experiment with service, cost, and risk measures.
units: Unit 1: Watch the process, productivity, and operations-strategy modules; draw a current-state process map.
Unit 2: Work capacity, bottleneck, and Little’s-law exercises in a spreadsheet.
Unit 3: Watch forecasting and inventory modules; create a demand forecast and safety-stock policy.
Unit 4: Watch quality, layout, and scheduling modules; conduct a root-cause and control-chart exercise.
Unit 5: Integrate supply-chain, technology, and sustainability risks into an improvement proposal.
courses.assignment: Deliver an operations diagnosis for a service or manufacturing workflow: process map, baseline data, bottleneck calculation, improvement experiment, and 90-day implementation plan.
courses.assessment: Rubric (100%): quantitative diagnosis 30; feasible process design 25; data/quality logic 20; risk and implementation 15; clarity 10.
courses.mapping: HBS Required Curriculum: Technology & Operations Management (TOM).

unitMap.text: Unit 1: Watch Weeks 1–2; define mission, vision, strategic plan, and strategic issue.
viewingSequence: Start with strategy and plan/tactics (L05), then planning/thinking (L06–L07); use vision (L11–L12), mission/values (L13), and process (L14–L15) to consolidate. The official NPTEL week placement puts explicit vision/mission lessons in Week 3, although the original MBA unit text says Weeks 1–2.
coveredTopics: company mission statement and core values
uncoveredTopics: framing and diagnosing a strategic issue as a distinct problem statement is not explicit in the indexed lecture titles
unitMap.practicalWork: Video viewing does not replace the assigned work: independently analyze a named organization and write the 2,500-word board strategy memo with an industry analysis, capability thesis, two alternatives, recommendation, and 12-month execution scorecard. Apply the original rubric: diagnosis 25%; strategic logic 30%; alternatives/trade-offs 20%; implementation realism 15%; evidence/writing 10%.

unitMap.text: Unit 2: Watch Weeks 3–5; complete PESTEL, five-forces, culture, and sustainability analyses.
viewingSequence: Begin with culture (L08), move to sustainability (L21–L22), then environment and strategy (L23–L24) and internal environment (L25). These titles establish broad environmental/sustainability coverage, not named PESTEL or five-forces instruction.
uncoveredTopics: a formal PESTEL analysis framework and its six dimensions
Porter’s Five Forces (rivalry, entrants, substitutes, buyers, suppliers) as a named industry-structure analysis
unitMap.practicalWork: Video viewing does not replace the assigned work: independently analyze a named organization and write the 2,500-word board strategy memo with an industry analysis, capability thesis, two alternatives, recommendation, and 12-month execution scorecard. Apply the original rubric: diagnosis 25%; strategic logic 30%; alternatives/trade-offs 20%; implementation realism 15%; evidence/writing 10%.

unitMap.text: Unit 3: Watch Weeks 6–8; assess resources, value chain, life cycle, and strategic alternatives.
viewingSequence: Proceed from resource-based analysis (L26) to capabilities/value chain (L27), then life cycle (L28), competition/red ocean (L29), blue-ocean sequence (L30–L34), and entrepreneurship/value creation (L35–L36).
coveredTopics: resources, capabilities, core competencies, and value chain
competitive strategy, red-ocean and blue-ocean alternatives
unitMap.practicalWork: Video viewing does not replace the assigned work: independently analyze a named organization and write the 2,500-word board strategy memo with an industry analysis, capability thesis, two alternatives, recommendation, and 12-month execution scorecard. Apply the original rubric: diagnosis 25%; strategic logic 30%; alternatives/trade-offs 20%; implementation realism 15%; evidence/writing 10%.

unitMap.text: Unit 4: Watch Weeks 9–10; select business/corporate scope and assess an acquisition.
viewingSequence: Start with business-level choices (L41–L42), then corporate-level design (L43–L46), competitive position (L47–L48), and finish with M&A (L49–L50). The videos support analysis; the learner still assesses a named organization/acquisition.
unitMap.practicalWork: Video viewing does not replace the assigned work: independently analyze a named organization and write the 2,500-word board strategy memo with an industry analysis, capability thesis, two alternatives, recommendation, and 12-month execution scorecard. Apply the original rubric: diagnosis 25%; strategic logic 30%; alternatives/trade-offs 20%; implementation realism 15%; evidence/writing 10%.

unitMap.text: Unit 5: Watch Weeks 11–12; design governance, implementation, and evaluation scorecard.
viewingSequence: Watch governance (L51–L53), operations and implementation (L54–L55), strategy evaluation (L56), then ESG/SDG (L58). The lectures provide concepts; the memo’s organization-specific 12-month scorecard must be built by the learner.
uncoveredTopics: designing a concrete 12-month execution scorecard with KPI definitions, targets, owners, milestones, and review cadence
unitMap.practicalWork: Video viewing does not replace the assigned work: independently analyze a named organization and write the 2,500-word board strategy memo with an industry analysis, capability thesis, two alternatives, recommendation, and 12-month execution scorecard. Apply the original rubric: diagnosis 25%; strategic logic 30%; alternatives/trade-offs 20%; implementation realism 15%; evidence/writing 10%.

remainingGaps: Unit 1: Direct instruction on framing and diagnosing a strategic issue as a distinct, evidence-based problem statement is not established by the official course titles; L14–L15 provide only broader process coverage.
Unit 2: No verified free university video in the primary series explicitly covers a formal PESTEL framework and its six dimensions; L23–L24 are broad environment/strategy coverage only.

Unit 2: No verified free university video in the primary series explicitly teaches Porter’s Five Forces; L23–L24 are partial general environment coverage. The authoritative Harvard Institute for Strategy and Competitiveness page explains the framework in text but is not a video, so it is not catalogued as a lecture: https://www.isc.hbs.edu/strategy/business-strategy/Pages/the-five-forces.aspx

Unit 5: No verified video explicitly walks through constructing an organization-specific 12-month execution scorecard with KPI definitions, targets, owners, milestones, and review cadence; L54–L56 are implementation/evaluation support, not a substitute for building the deliverable.

courses.title: Leadership & Organizational Behavior
courses.level: MBA core mapping; external IIT series is a broad substitute. Leadership practice is self-directed rather than HBS section-based.
courses.prerequisites: None; willingness to solicit feedback and keep a reflection journal.
objectives: Explain how perception, personality, motivation, and emotion shape work behavior.
Diagnose power, leadership, communication, group dynamics, and culture.
Practice a feedback, coaching, and conflict conversation using evidence.
Design a change intervention and personal leadership-development plan.
units: Unit 1: Watch Weeks 1–4; complete a perception/personality reflection and observation log.
Unit 2: Watch Weeks 5–6; diagnose motivation and emotion in a real work setting.
Unit 3: Watch Weeks 7–9; practice a communication and decision-making protocol with peers.
Unit 4: Watch Week 10; prepare and record a leadership, power, or feedback conversation.
Unit 5: Watch Weeks 11–12; analyze culture and propose a change intervention with safeguards.
courses.assignment: Submit a leadership portfolio: stakeholder feedback summary, two recorded/practiced difficult conversations, a team-dynamics diagnosis, and a 90-day development plan with measurable behaviors.
courses.assessment: Rubric (100%): candid evidence and reflection 25; OB diagnosis 30; applied communication/leadership skill 25; development-plan specificity 20.
courses.mapping: HBS Required Curriculum: Leadership & Organizational Behavior (LEAD).

unitMap.text: Unit 1: Watch Weeks 1–4; complete a perception/personality reflection and observation log.
viewingSequence: Weeks 1–2: P01–P09, foundations and perception.
Weeks 3–4: P10–P22, personality, learning, then attitudes.
coveredTopics: organizational-behavior foundations and levels of analysis
personality and individual differences at work
unitMap.practicalWork: Complete the assigned perception/personality reflection and observation log; videos supply concepts, not the learner’s observations or reflection.

unitMap.text: Unit 2: Watch Weeks 5–6; diagnose motivation and emotion in a real work setting.
viewingSequence: Week 5: P23–P25, emotions.
Week 6: P26–P31, motivation.
coveredTopics: motivation concepts and theories as developed in the six-part series
application of motivation/emotion concepts to workplace behavior
unitMap.practicalWork: Diagnose motivation and emotion in an actual work setting; viewing does not replace field observation or evidence gathering.

unitMap.text: Unit 3: Watch Weeks 7–9; practice a communication and decision-making protocol with peers.
viewingSequence: Week 7: P32–P35, interpersonal relationships.
Week 8: P36–P38, communication.
Week 9: P39–P42, decision making.
Then S01 followed by S02 for direct instruction in conflict management and negotiation (IIT Kharagpur NPTEL topic-matched substitute).
coveredTopics: organizational/intergroup conflict, causes and functional/dysfunctional effects (supplement)
uncoveredTopics: A verified, explicit, evidence-based step-by-step script or simulation of an interpersonal difficult/conflict conversation; the public conflict lectures teach conflict and negotiation concepts, not a demonstrated conversation protocol.
unitMap.practicalWork: The communication/decision protocol with peers and the evidence-based conflict-conversation practice are learner work; use a real case, obtain peer practice/feedback, and do not substitute viewing for the role-play.

unitMap.text: Unit 4: Watch Week 10; prepare and record a leadership, power, or feedback conversation.
viewingSequence: Week 10: P43–P47, power and leadership.
Then S03 for a focused workplace coaching/feedback supplement.
coveredTopics: leadership behavior and influence as presented across the five-part unit
coaching skills, coachability, application, and accountability (supplement)
unitMap.practicalWork: Prepare and record/practice the leadership, power, or feedback conversation. S03 is a university professional-development webinar, not a credential or a substitute for the learner’s recorded practice.

unitMap.text: Unit 5: Watch Weeks 11–12; analyze culture and propose a change intervention with safeguards.
viewingSequence: Week 11: P48–P50 group dynamics, then P51–P52 organizational culture.
Week 12: P53 organizational change, then P54–P56 organizational structure.
coveredTopics: organizational change at an introductory/topic level
uncoveredTopics: A specifically verified lecture on designing a change intervention with explicit safeguards, stakeholder-risk controls, and evaluation measures; the indexed change lecture is broad and does not separately evidence these design details.
unitMap.practicalWork: The culture diagnosis and change-intervention proposal with safeguards remain learner work; provide evidence and justify safeguards using course readings/research rather than inferring that the video covers them.

remainingGaps: Unit 3: No verified public recording in this catalogue demonstrates an evidence-based, step-by-step difficult/conflict conversation script or simulation. NPTEL IIT Kharagpur S01–S02 are verified concept-level coverage of organizational conflict and negotiation, not a conversation rehearsal. The University of Minnesota difficult-conversations page summarizes a webinar but does not expose a verified direct playable recording in the inspected page; it is therefore not counted as a video.

Unit 5: The public/indexed course material provides a broad Organizational Change lecture (P53), but no specifically verified lecture on change-intervention safeguards, stakeholder-risk controls, or evaluation measures. Preserve and complete that part of the assignment through learner-led evidence/research.

Unit 3: A verified, explicit, evidence-based step-by-step script or simulation of an interpersonal difficult/conflict conversation; the public conflict lectures teach conflict and negotiation concepts, not a demonstrated conversation protocol.

Unit 5: A specifically verified lecture on designing a change intervention with explicit safeguards, stakeholder-risk controls, and evaluation measures; the indexed change lecture is broad and does not separately evidence these design details.

courses.title: Data Science & AI for Leaders
courses.level: MBA core mapping; MIT 15.071 is a graduate Sloan analytics course. It predates some current generative-AI practice, so responsible GenAI governance is an explicit topic gap addressed in the assignment and HarvardX supplement.
courses.prerequisites: Spreadsheet fluency; basic probability helpful. Complete a short R/Python orientation before Unit 2.
objectives: Frame a business decision as prediction, optimization, simulation, or experiment.
Interpret regression, classification, clustering, and optimization outputs.
Evaluate model performance, overfitting, data quality, and deployment risk.
Propose an AI-enabled decision workflow with human oversight and fairness controls.
units: Unit 1: Complete the introduction and R orientation; convert one business question into a measurable outcome.
Unit 2: Work regression and sports-analytics examples; evaluate an out-of-sample prediction.
Unit 3: Work logistic-regression and risk-factor modules; create a confusion matrix and threshold policy.
Unit 4: Work text, clustering, and visualization modules; make a decision-ready customer insight.
Unit 5: Work linear/integer optimization modules; write a model card, governance plan, and human-review rule.
courses.assignment: Build a small decision prototype using lawful public or self-collected data. Submit reproducible analysis, model/performance results, a model card, risk/fairness review, and executive recommendation; no sensitive personal data.
courses.assessment: Rubric (100%): framing/data fitness 20; method and validation 30; decision value 20; governance/ethics 20; reproducibility 10.
courses.mapping: HBS Required Curriculum: Data Science & AI for Leaders (DSAIL).

lectures.title: The Three Laws of AI — Lecture 7
lectures.provider: MIT 6.S191: Introduction to Deep Learning (MIT) / MIT Deep Learning

unitMap.text: Unit 1: Complete the introduction and R orientation; convert one business question into a measurable outcome.
viewingSequence: MIT 15.071 Unit 1 analytics framing examples, then the complete Unit 1 R/data-orientation and food-data recitation lessons in their official sequence.
coveredTopics: Turning an applied question into an analytics problem and identifying a measurable target/outcome, with real-world analytics examples.
R orientation for vectors/data frames, loading data, summary statistics, scatterplots, plots/tables, adding variables, and saving reproducible scripts.
Exploratory summaries and plots as an initial check of business data.
uncoveredTopics: A systematic decision-framing lesson that distinguishes prediction, optimization, simulation, and causal experimentation, including experimental design/randomization, is not verified in this public lecture inventory.
unitMap.practicalWork: Complete the original individual practice: convert one business question into a measurable outcome; install/use R or Python as needed and inspect lawful data. Video viewing does not perform the framing or data work.

unitMap.text: Unit 2: Work regression and sports-analytics examples; evaluate an out-of-sample prediction.
viewingSequence: MIT 15.071 Unit 2: linear-regression/wine lessons first, followed by the Moneyball/sports-analytics lessons and recitation. Then use the indexed Unit 4 CART/tree, train/test split, cross-validation, prediction-error, baseline/penalty-matrix, and pruning lessons as the explicit out-of-sample validation extension; finish by evaluating a held-out prediction in the learner assignment.
coveredTopics: Linear regression: fitting and interpreting one-variable and multiple-variable models, and interpreting regression output in the wine-quality case.
Sports analytics and Moneyball-style prediction examples, including applying predictions to decisions.
Out-of-sample prediction and validation ideas as applied in the MIT regression/sports sequence; validate with a held-out sample in the learner assignment.

Decision-tree/CART and random-forest model examples; train/test splitting, cross-validation, prediction error measures, baseline/penalty-matrix comparison, and pruning-complexity validation for out-of-sample generalization.
unitMap.practicalWork: Complete the original individual assignment/practice using the lessons: reproduce the relevant analysis, interpret model/optimization output, validate decisions, and document reasoning. Video viewing does not substitute for learner analysis.

unitMap.text: Unit 3: Work logistic-regression and risk-factor modules; create a confusion matrix and threshold policy.
viewingSequence: MIT 15.071 Unit 3: logistic-regression lessons, then Framingham risk-factor lessons, then the election-forecasting recitation; finish by constructing the assigned confusion matrix and threshold policy.
coveredTopics: Logistic regression for binary classification and probability/risk-factor modeling.
Modeling expert decisions and cardiovascular risk in the Framingham study.
Classification trade-offs and evaluating predicted risks; translate a threshold into an explicit confusion-matrix/policy exercise.
unitMap.practicalWork: Complete the original individual assignment/practice using the lessons: reproduce the relevant analysis, interpret model/optimization output, validate decisions, and document reasoning. Video viewing does not substitute for learner analysis.

unitMap.text: Unit 4: Work text, clustering, and visualization modules; make a decision-ready customer insight.
viewingSequence: MIT 15.071 Unit 5 text analytics → Unit 6 clustering/recommendation → Unit 7 visualization and visualization recitation, in playlist order.
coveredTopics: Text analytics: sentiment detection, text mining, IBM Watson question answering, and predictive coding.
Clustering and recommendation/customer segmentation, including Netflix and health-pattern examples; recitation material compares clustering approaches.
Visualization: exploratory and decision-facing charts, scatterplots, line plots, heat maps, geographical displays, and critique of visual design.
unitMap.practicalWork: Complete the original individual assignment/practice using the lessons: reproduce the relevant analysis, interpret model/optimization output, validate decisions, and document reasoning. Video viewing does not substitute for learner analysis.

unitMap.text: Unit 5: Work linear/integer optimization modules; write a model card, governance plan, and human-review rule.
viewingSequence: MIT 15.071 Unit 8 linear optimization (revenue management, radiation therapy, AdWords) → Unit 9 integer optimization (sports schedules, eHarmony, operating rooms); then MIT 6.S191 2021 Bias and Fairness → MIT 6.S191 2026 The Three Laws of AI. Write the model card/governance materials yourself.
coveredTopics: Linear optimization: decision variables, objective/constraints, formulation, solution, sensitivity, and revenue-management/advertising/radiation-therapy examples.
Integer optimization: binary/logical constraints, schedules, matching/compatibility and operational scheduling.
Fairness, sources of algorithmic bias, subgroup performance concerns, mitigation ideas, and contemporary AI safety/evaluation themes (MIT 6.S191 supplements).
uncoveredTopics: A practical model-card template and organization-level deployment governance/control process, including explicit accountable human-review/escalation rules, are not fully taught in a verified public lecture.
Manager-focused generative-AI governance, privacy/provenance, and deployment-risk evaluation remain incomplete; the safety lecture is a supplement, not a complete governance standard.
unitMap.practicalWork: The prototype, reproducible analysis, model/performance results, model card, risk/fairness review, and executive recommendation remain learner work; use lawful public or self-collected data and no sensitive personal data. Neither lectures nor supplements complete this capstone deliverable or create a credential.

remainingGaps: Unit 1 / course objective: no verified public lecture in this inventory fully teaches decision framing across prediction, optimization, simulation, and causal experiments, including experimental design and randomization.

Unit 5: no verified public lecture supplies a practical model-card template and complete organization-level deployment governance workflow with accountable human-review/escalation rules. MIT 6.S191 fairness and safety lectures are useful but partial.

Unit 5: current generative-AI governance, data provenance/privacy, and manager-level deployment evaluation remain incomplete; the MIT safety demonstration does not substitute for the responsible-GenAI controls required by the assignment.

courses.level: MBA core mapping; MIT 14.02 is explicitly undergraduate and is therefore a prerequisite/substitute resource, not graduate MBA instruction.
courses.prerequisites: High-school algebra; no prior macroeconomics assumed.
objectives: Explain output, inflation, unemployment, growth, and business-cycle mechanisms.
Analyze monetary, fiscal, exchange-rate, and trade-policy effects on a firm.

unitMap.text: Unit 1: Watch lectures 1–5; build a national-income and financial-market concept map.
viewingSequence: MBA108-L01 — establish the macroeconomic scope.
MBA108-L02 — acquire basic macroeconomic concepts and measurement.
MBA108-L03 — connect spending, production, income and equilibrium output in the goods market.
MBA108-L04 — introduce the financial market.
MBA108-L05 — synthesize goods/financial markets in IS–LM.
MBA108-S01 — supplement with bank intermediation, liquidity, runs and regulation.
coveredTopics: Macroeconomic scope and core aggregates / economic measurement
National-income and output concepts; goods-market demand, production and equilibrium
Financial-market foundations and the interaction of goods and financial markets
Credit intermediation, liquidity provision, adverse selection, moral hazard, bank runs and prudential regulation (supplement)
unitMap.practicalWork: Learner still creates the national-income/financial-market concept map; viewing does not complete the synthesis.

unitMap.text: Unit 2: Watch lectures 6–10; diagnose an inflation/unemployment episode with data.
viewingSequence: MBA108-L06 — continue IS–LM and short-run fluctuations.
MBA108-L07 — extend the IS–LM model.
MBA108-L08 — study labor-market outcomes and unemployment.
MBA108-L09 — study the Phillips curve and inflation.
MBA108-L10 — use the review as recap after the substantive lectures.
coveredTopics: Short-run output fluctuations and extended IS–LM mechanisms
Mechanisms needed to interpret an inflation/unemployment episode
unitMap.practicalWork: The learner must select an actual episode and suitable data, diagnose it, and distinguish evidence from interpretation; the review video is not the data exercise.

unitMap.text: Unit 3: Watch lectures 11–15; model fiscal and monetary-policy transmission to a company.
viewingSequence: MBA108-L05 — use IS–LM foundations for demand and interest-rate policy channels.
MBA108-L06 — continue policy transmission through output and financial markets.
MBA108-L07 — extend the model before the assigned block.
MBA108-L11 — connect IS–LM with the Phillips curve.
MBA108-L12 — continue the IS–LM-PC adjustment process.
MBA108-L13 — place policy choices against long-run growth facts.
MBA108-L14 — study saving and capital accumulation.
MBA108-L15 — study technological progress and growth.
MBA108-L22 and MBA108-L24 — add financial-market expectations and policy expectations when modeling a company scenario.
coveredTopics: Monetary/interest-rate channels through financial markets, output and inflation expectations
IS–LM / IS–LM-PC policy transmission and short-run adjustment
Long-run output, saving, capital accumulation and productivity context for company planning
uncoveredTopics: A clearly identified full lecture on fiscal instrument design and the detailed firm-level transmission of alternative tax-versus-spending choices, fiscal multipliers/leakages and public-debt sustainability; policy-model lectures provide only partial support.
unitMap.practicalWork: Learner must build the company-specific transmission model and state assumptions. MIT class topic/readings materials list fiscal policy, but no gallery recording title identifies a dedicated fiscal-policy session; do not infer detailed treatment from titles alone.

unitMap.text: Unit 4: Watch lectures 16–20; analyze exchange rates, trade exposure, and global capital flows.
viewingSequence: MBA108-L16 — frame cross-country differences.
MBA108-L17 — introduce the open economy.
MBA108-L19 — study the goods market in an open economy and net-export channel.
MBA108-L20 — study the Mundell–Fleming model and cross-border policy/capital-mobility mechanisms.
MBA108-L21 — compare exchange-rate regimes (assigned next block; bring forward for this unit).
MBA108-L18 — use the quiz review after the substantive coverage.
coveredTopics: Cross-border capital-mobility mechanisms in the Mundell–Fleming framework
uncoveredTopics: Explicit trade-policy instruments (tariffs, quotas, trade agreements and restrictions) and a dedicated firm supply-chain/trade-policy incidence treatment; the available course lectures cover open-economy goods flows, not a full trade-policy module.
unitMap.practicalWork: Learner must identify a real firm’s cross-border revenue, cost, sourcing and financing exposures and quantify them; the videos provide macroeconomic mechanisms, not a company exposure analysis.

unitMap.text: Unit 5: Watch lectures 21–25; write a country-and-policy scenario for a management team.
viewingSequence: MBA108-L21 — review exchange-rate regimes and policy choices.
MBA108-L22 — study financial markets and expectations.
MBA108-L23 — connect macro-financial conditions to asset pricing.
MBA108-L24 — study expectations in IS–LM and policy.
MBA108-L25 — use the final review after the topic lectures.
coveredTopics: Financial markets, expectations and asset pricing
Policy expectations and macro-financial scenario mechanisms
unitMap.practicalWork: The country-risk/policy brief is learner work. Independently select current indicators, construct baseline and alternative shocks/policy scenarios, explain uncertainty and stakeholders, and recommend firm actions; no lecture substitutes for the 1,800-word assignment or its rubric.

remainingGaps: Unit 3: The verified recordings do not clearly provide a dedicated full lecture on fiscal instrument design (tax versus spending composition, multipliers/leakages, debt sustainability) and detailed firm-level transmission. MIT course topic materials list fiscal policy, but the public lecture gallery does not identify a dedicated recording; treat IS–LM coverage as partial.

Unit 4: No verified full lecture in the selected series directly teaches tariffs, quotas, trade agreements/restrictions, and firm supply-chain incidence as trade-policy instruments. The MIT open-economy lectures cover net exports, exchange rates and capital mobility, not the complete trade-policy gap.

Unit 3: A clearly identified full lecture on fiscal instrument design and the detailed firm-level transmission of alternative tax-versus-spending choices, fiscal multipliers/leakages and public-debt sustainability; policy-model lectures provide only partial support.

Unit 4: Explicit trade-policy instruments (tariffs, quotas, trade agreements and restrictions) and a dedicated firm supply-chain/trade-policy incidence treatment; the available course lectures cover open-economy goods flows, not a full trade-policy module.

unitMap.text: Unit 1: Watch lectures 1–7; map risk-sharing institutions and diversify a sample portfolio.
viewingSequence: Y252-L01 → Y252-L02 for course framing and financial risk/crisis foundations.
Y252-L03 → Y252-L04 for financial institutions/innovation and portfolio diversification.
Y252-L05 → Y252-L06 → Y252-L07 for insurance, institutional portfolio practice and efficient markets.
coveredTopics: Financial risk and crisis probability; dependence, correlation, portfolio risk and fat-tailed outcomes.
Risk-sharing institutions and financial innovation; insurance as a risk-management institution.
Diversification, portfolio risk-return trade-offs, efficient frontiers, CAPM and efficient markets.
unitMap.practicalWork: The sample-portfolio mapping and diversification exercise is learner work; lectures explain concepts but do not complete the exercise.

unitMap.text: Unit 2: Watch lectures 8–14; analyze debt, stocks, real estate, behavioral bias, banks, and a crisis.
viewingSequence: Y252-L08 → Y252-L09 → Y252-L10 for debt, equity and real estate.
Y252-L11 → Y252-L12 for behavioral bias, crisis, misconduct and regulation.
Y252-L13 → Y252-L14 for bank/intermediary and insurance-industry perspectives.
FR-03 → FR-04 for public-policy response and post-crisis lessons; use as supplements after Yale’s crisis/regulation lecture.
Return to Y252-L02 for probabilistic risk and systemic/tail-risk context.
coveredTopics: Debt and bond valuation, interest rates, leverage cycles and consumer-finance context.
Corporate stocks and real estate as financial assets.
Financial crises, regulation and bank institutions; risk concepts including systemic/idiosyncratic risk, dependence and tail risk.
Central-bank crisis response and post-crisis policy/regulation (supplementary).
uncoveredTopics: Dedicated contemporary credit-risk measurement and underwriting (for example, default probability, loss given default, exposure at default, and portfolio concentration) is not systematically taught by these verified lectures.
Bank funding/liquidity-risk metrics and liquidity stress-testing frameworks are not covered in sufficient detail for a complete applied risk-management treatment.
unitMap.practicalWork: The learner must perform the unit’s crisis and market analysis. The video evidence is an undergraduate Yale substitute for an HBS MBA course, not HBS credit; historical lectures are not a current regulatory update.

unitMap.text: Unit 3: Watch lectures 15–18; value/diagram futures and options and examine monetary-policy channels.
viewingSequence: Y252-L15 for forward/futures contract mechanics and hedging.
Y252-L17 for option structures, valuation and volatility.
Y252-L18 → FR-04 for monetary-policy channels and crisis-era policy context.
Y252-L16 is an optional in-sequence practitioner perspective on international financial markets.
coveredTopics: Forward and futures markets and hedging.
Option contract payoffs, calls/puts, put-call parity, binomial and Black–Scholes valuation, implied volatility.
Monetary policy and financial-market channels; supplemental post-crisis monetary-policy context.
unitMap.practicalWork: The learner must value and diagram the assigned futures/options examples; viewing alone does not perform the calculations or establish a hedge recommendation.

unitMap.text: Unit 4: Watch lectures 19–23; assess intermediaries, exchanges, public finance, and financial purpose.
viewingSequence: Y252-L19 → Y252-L20 for investment banks and professional money managers.
Y252-L21 for exchanges, brokers, dealers and clearing/settlement infrastructure.
Y252-L22 → Y252-L23 for public/nonprofit finance and financial purpose.
coveredTopics: Investment banks and professional money managers/intermediaries.
Financial capitalism, purpose and social consequences.
unitMap.practicalWork: The learner must independently assess institutional choices and their consequences; the lecture series is conceptual instruction, not an industry placement or HBS field experience.

unitMap.text: Unit 5: Consolidate transcript notes into a market-risk briefing with regulatory and ethical implications.
viewingSequence: Revisit relevant mechanism lectures: Y252-L02, Y252-L08, Y252-L13, Y252-L18, Y252-L19 and Y252-L21.
Then review Y252-L12 and FR-03 → FR-04 for regulatory and crisis-response implications.
Finish with Y252-L22 → Y252-L23 to frame public purpose and social/ethical consequences before writing.
coveredTopics: Market-risk mechanisms, debt/financing, institutional exposures and monetary-policy context.
Regulatory/governance implications and post-crisis policy response.
Public purpose, social consequences and ethical framing of financial decisions.
unitMap.practicalWork: The 2,000-word board risk brief is assessed learner work: create the exposure map, scenario triggers, compare hedge/financing alternatives, formulate controls and recommendation, and cite sources. Videos support learning but do not substitute for the assignment or rubric.

remainingGaps: Unit 2 remains partial: the verified Yale and Federal Reserve public videos give strong foundational coverage of crisis risk, debt, banks and policy, but do not systematically teach contemporary credit-risk quantification (PD/LGD/EAD, underwriting/concentration) or bank funding-liquidity metrics and stress testing. A targeted search found an IIT Kharagpur NPTEL commercial-banking course listing those subjects, but its public preview did not expose verified individual playable lecture links; it is therefore not catalogued as video evidence.

courses.title: Leadership, Corporate Accountability & Purpose of the Firm
courses.level: MBA core mapping; NPTEL business-ethics series is an external professional substitute. It does not supply HBS cases or cohort debate.
courses.prerequisites: MBA-101 and MBA-106 recommended.
objectives: Apply ethical theories and stakeholder analysis to corporate choices.
Design accountability, governance, reporting, and speak-up mechanisms.
Reconcile shareholder, employee, customer, community, and environmental claims.
Articulate a credible firm purpose and test it against incentives and performance measures.
units: Unit 1: Watch lectures 1–9; define ethics, corporation, CSR, stakeholder theory, and accountability.
Unit 2: Watch lectures 10–21; apply ethical theory and a decision model to a contested management choice.
Unit 3: Watch lectures 22–32; evaluate governance, ownership, finance, and employment obligations.
Unit 4: Watch lectures 33–53; analyze consumer, supplier, civil-society, and government relationships.
Unit 5: Watch lectures 54–61; write environmental and data/technology governance commitments.
courses.assignment: Develop a board-ready accountability charter for a real organization: purpose statement, stakeholder materiality map, governance/control design, metrics, escalation path, and a 1,500-word ethical decision memorandum.
courses.assessment: Rubric (100%): stakeholder/ethical analysis 30; accountable governance design 25; purpose-incentive alignment 20; metrics and escalation 15; clarity 10.
courses.mapping: HBS Required Curriculum: Leadership & Corporate Accountability (LCA) and Purpose of the Firm. This intentionally combines two HBS spring-area requirements in one integrated course.

courses.title: Elective: Negotiation, Competition & Strategic Interaction
courses.level: Elective; Yale ECON 159 is an undergraduate prerequisite/substitute. Complete MBA-105 or equivalent first.
courses.prerequisites: MBA-105 and basic probability; calculus is helpful but not necessary for the managerial applications.
objectives: Use dominance, best response, Nash equilibrium, and backward induction in strategic choices.
Diagnose credibility, commitment, bargaining, repeated games, and incentives.
Recognize asymmetric information, signaling, adverse selection, and auction risk.
Convert a game-theoretic analysis into a practical negotiation or competitive move.
units: Unit 1: Watch lectures 1–5; solve dominance, beliefs, best-response, and equilibrium games.
Unit 2: Watch lectures 6–12; practice mixed strategies, evolution, and coordination settings.
Unit 3: Watch lectures 13–18; model sequential choices, commitments, threats, and bargaining.
Unit 4: Watch lectures 19–24; analyze repeated games, outsourcing, signaling, and auctions.
Unit 5: Run a negotiated simulation, write a game tree, and turn it into a managerial playbook.
courses.assignment: Submit a negotiation/competitive strategy memo with a game tree, equilibrium analysis, information assumptions, credible commitments, two ethical constraints, and a debrief from one live simulation.
courses.assessment: Rubric (100%): correct model 35; interpretation/assumptions 25; actionable strategy 20; negotiation reflection 10; ethics/clarity 10.
courses.mapping: Elective curriculum: Negotiation, Organizations & Markets / strategy and decision-making enrichment. It also deepens economics; it is not a replacement for a named HBS required course.

unitMap.text: Unit 1: Watch lectures 1–5; solve dominance, beliefs, best-response, and equilibrium games.
viewingSequence: Y01 for game elements, dominance, and coordination; Y02 for reasoning about others’ beliefs and choices.
Y03 for iterative deletion; Y04 for best responses; Y05 for Nash equilibrium and bank-run coordination.
coveredTopics: beliefs about other players and strategic reasoning
unitMap.practicalWork: Solve the stated dominance, belief, best-response, and equilibrium games yourself; lecture viewing is not a substitute for the assigned problem solving.

unitMap.text: Unit 2: Watch lectures 6–12; practice mixed strategies, evolution, and coordination settings.
viewingSequence: Y06–Y08 in order for Nash equilibrium applications, coordination, location, segregation, and randomization.
Y09–Y10 for mixed strategies and applied examples.
Y11–Y12 for evolutionary stability, convention, aggression, and cycles.
unitMap.practicalWork: Work the mixed-strategy and coordination exercises independently; examples in the recordings do not replace practice.

unitMap.text: Unit 3: Watch lectures 13–18; model sequential choices, commitments, threats, and bargaining.
viewingSequence: Y13 for sequential games, moral hazard, and incentives.
Y14–Y16 for backward induction, commitment, credible threats, first-mover advantage, and reputation.
Y17 for ultimatums and bargaining; then M09 and M11 as matched MIT negotiation/bargaining supplements.
Y18 for imperfect information, information sets, and subgame perfection.
unitMap.practicalWork: The videos supply analysis frameworks; apply them to original games and negotiation scenarios yourself.

unitMap.text: Unit 4: Watch lectures 19–24; analyze repeated games, outsourcing, signaling, and auctions.
viewingSequence: Y19–Y20 for subgame-perfect equilibrium, strategic investment, and attrition.
Y21–Y22 for repeated cooperation, end games, cheating, punishment, and outsourcing; deepen with M12–M13.
Y23 for asymmetric information and signaling; extend in sequence M16, M17, M21, M22, then M24.
Y24 for auctions, common/private values, and the winner’s curse; deepen with M18.
M23 extends bargaining to incomplete information.
coveredTopics: strategic investment and wars of attrition
repeated games, cooperation, end-game incentives, cheating, and punishment
unitMap.practicalWork: Use these lectures to analyze a new competitive setting; independently check assumptions about information and payoffs.

unitMap.text: Unit 5: Run a negotiated simulation, write a game tree, and turn it into a managerial playbook.
viewingSequence: Revisit Y04 for best-response analysis in business partnerships and Y14 for commitment/credible moves.
Use Y17 and M09 for bargaining/negotiation frameworks; M23 extends bargaining under private information.
Use Y22 for repeated interaction and outsourcing incentives; then create and analyze the game tree before the live simulation.
coveredTopics: applying best-response analysis to business partnerships
translating game-theoretic analysis into a managerial move
uncoveredTopics: Dedicated, explicit negotiation-ethics framework for developing and assessing the assignment’s two ethical constraints is not covered by a verified public recording. Yale Y17 and MIT M09/M23 provide strategic bargaining context only.
unitMap.practicalWork: Learner must run the negotiated simulation, construct the game tree, write the memo/playbook, identify two ethical constraints, and complete the debrief. Video viewing cannot substitute for participation, authorship, ethical judgment, or reflection.

remainingGaps: Unit 5: No verified publicly playable university lecture was found that explicitly teaches a negotiation-ethics framework for formulating and assessing the memo’s two ethical constraints. MIT OCW 15.067 describes ethics dilemmas in negotiation but its public course site publishes notes and activity assignments rather than lecture recordings; Yale Y17 and MIT M09/M23 provide partial strategic-bargaining context only. The live simulation, game tree, memo/playbook, ethical judgment, and debrief remain learner work.

courses.title: Elective: Capitalism, Institutions & Sustainable Value
courses.level: Elective; Yale PLSC 270 is undergraduate and interdisciplinary. It is a broad substitute, not a current MBA seminar.
courses.prerequisites: MBA-108 and MBA-111 recommended.
objectives: Compare institutional accounts of capitalism, property, corporate organization, and public purpose.
Analyze poverty, development, environmental, public-health, and financial-crisis consequences.
Assess how government, law, and civil society shape firm incentives.
Defend a sustainable-value proposal with historical and stakeholder evidence.
units: Unit 1: Watch lectures 1–6; compare Malthus, Smith, Marx, Schumpeter, property, and corporations.
Unit 2: Watch lectures 7–12; analyze health markets, technology life cycles, finance, and accountability.
Unit 3: Watch lectures 13–18; examine law, affluence, poverty, and microfinance.
Unit 4: Watch lectures 19–24; evaluate development policy and a clean-water enterprise case.
Unit 5: Write a policy/enterprise design that makes explicit its social objective and trade-offs.
courses.assignment: Write three 800–1,000-word memoranda on a local or global capitalism issue, then synthesize them into a 2,000-word sustainable-value policy-and-business recommendation.
courses.assessment: Rubric (100%): institutional reasoning 30; evidence and historical context 20; stakeholder/policy design 25; trade-offs 15; writing 10.
courses.mapping: Elective curriculum: Business, Government & the International Economy / General Management enrichment; extends BGIE and Purpose of the Firm.

unitMap.text: Unit 1: Watch lectures 1–6; compare Malthus, Smith, Marx, Schumpeter, property, and corporations.
viewingSequence: Y270-01 — establish capital/capitalism and the course frame.
Y270-02 — Malthus, population pressure, and inevitable poverty.
Y270-03 — Smith’s invisible hand, market preconditions, competition, and moral limits.
Y270-04 — Marx, Schumpeter, instability, and creative destruction.
Y270-05 — freedom, government, property rights, and de Soto.
Y270-06 — rise of the joint-stock corporation.

Malthusian account of population and poverty
Adam Smith’s market coordination, market preconditions, and moral framing
Marxian critique and Schumpeterian creative destruction

Joint-stock corporation as a business form

unitMap.text: Unit 2: Watch lectures 7–12; analyze health markets, technology life cycles, finance, and accountability.

unitMap.practicalWork: Case viewing does not replace independent case analysis. No proprietary HBS case packet is supplied or represented as openly available.

unitMap.text: Unit 3: Watch lectures 13–18; examine law, affluence, poverty, and microfinance.
viewingSequence: Y270-13 — mortgage meltdown and local consequences in Cleveland.
Y270-14 — political and judicial foundations of American capitalism.
Y270-15 — historical arrival of mass affluence in the Western world.
Y270-16 — formal/informal property, development policy, transaction costs, and the limits of GDP-led investment.
Y270-17 — poverty and capitalism through the Balram Halwai case.
Y270-18 — SELCO, rural energy access, microfinance partnership, and business-model trade-offs.
coveredTopics: Political and judicial institutions shaping capitalism
Property regimes, development constraints, and transaction costs
Poverty as experienced by people at the bottom of the income distribution
Microfinance-linked enterprise, rural energy access, and operating-model trade-offs
unitMap.practicalWork: The learner must independently assess the cases and support memoranda with evidence; videos do not provide a guaranteed case-study answer.

unitMap.text: Unit 4: Watch lectures 19–24; evaluate development policy and a clean-water enterprise case.
viewingSequence: Y270-19 — GDP limits, bottom-billion poverty traps, aid/trade policy, resource curse, and institutions for reform.
Y270-20 — policy targets for capitalist development and the interaction of government with enterprise.
Y270-21 — Goldman Sachs partnership/corporate-form incentives and relationships with government and society.
Y270-22 — European utility acquisition, regional politics, governments, and market operations.
Y270-23 — TXU private-equity deal, environmental groups, public opinion, and stakeholder coalitions.
Y270-24 — course synthesis and the Bechtel/Cochabamba clean-water enterprise case.

courses.title: FIELD-Style Action Learning & Integrative Business Capstone
courses.level: Capstone. NPTEL Project Management for Managers is a broad external lecture-series foundation. The topic gap is material: it cannot supply an HBS faculty-sponsored company project, global immersion, team cohort, or live FIELD feedback. The learner must source a lawful host organization or use an independently scoped public-interest/client project.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of at least ten prior courses; all 13 prior courses strongly recommended. Obtain informed consent before collecting company/customer data.
objectives: Scope, govern, and execute a cross-functional business project with a real decision owner.
Integrate market, operations, finance, data, leadership, policy, and ethics evidence.
Use milestones, risks, stakeholder management, and learning loops to deliver results.
Present an investment/implementation recommendation and reflect on leadership impact.
units: Phase 1 (Weeks 1–4): secure a sponsor, write problem charter, stakeholder map, data/ethics plan, and success metrics.
Phase 2 (Weeks 5–8): conduct customer/market/operations/finance diagnosis and define a baseline.
Phase 3 (Weeks 9–14): generate alternatives, test a prototype or process change, and update a risk register.
Phase 4 (Weeks 15–20): build implementation, resource, governance, and change-management plan.
Phase 5 (Weeks 21–24): deliver sponsor presentation, executive memo, artifact handover, and reflective after-action review.
courses.assignment: Complete a sponsor-facing capstone (minimum 120 hours): charter; evidence pack; financial/operational model; market and stakeholder analysis; ethical/data review; prototype or implementation plan; 12–15 page executive report; 10-minute presentation; sponsor or peer feedback; and a personal leadership reflection.
courses.assessment: Rubric (100%): problem/evidence quality 20; cross-functional analysis 25; solution and feasibility 20; ethics/stakeholder/governance 15; communication and sponsor feedback 10; reflection/learning 10.
courses.mapping: HBS FIELD-style experiential learning, summer-work analogue, and integrative business capstone. It synthesizes FRC, FIN, MKT, TOM, STRAT, LEAD, DSAIL, BGIE, TEM, LCA, and electives.

unitMap.text: Phase 1 (Weeks 1–4): secure a sponsor, write problem charter, stakeholder map, data/ethics plan, and success metrics.
viewingSequence: Start with L01–L05 for project context, success, organization/PMO, and stakeholders. Lecture IDs: MBA114-L01, MBA114-L02, MBA114-L03, MBA114-L04, MBA114-L05
Then L33–L34 for scheduling and project time-management framing. Lecture IDs: MBA114-L33, MBA114-L34
coveredTopics: project management introduction and success criteria (L01–L02)
organizational structures and project management office (L03–L04)
project time-management framing and scheduling introduction (L33–L34)
uncoveredTopics: securing a real decision-owner sponsor and negotiating a project charter
consent, privacy, data-governance and ethics plan for company/customer evidence
designing and validating project-specific success metrics and sponsor feedback loops
unitMap.practicalWork: Videos provide concepts; the learner must secure a lawful host/sponsor and produce the charter, stakeholder map, data/ethics plan, and metrics in practice.

unitMap.text: Phase 2 (Weeks 5–8): conduct customer/market/operations/finance diagnosis and define a baseline.
viewingSequence: Begin with L06–L07 for lifecycle and appraisal. Lecture IDs: MBA114-L06, MBA114-L07
Then L13–L14 for market and demand analysis. Lecture IDs: MBA114-L13, MBA114-L14
Then L15–L18 for financial analysis, capital budgeting, and project finance. Lecture IDs: MBA114-L15, MBA114-L16, MBA114-L17, MBA114-L18
Finish L29–L30 for technical analysis and product/plant capacity. Lecture IDs: MBA114-L29, MBA114-L30
coveredTopics: project life-cycle phases and project appraisal (L06–L07)
uncoveredTopics: customer discovery and primary research design
collecting a project-specific market/operations baseline and validating data quality
integrating market, operations, finance, data, leadership, policy, and ethics evidence in a sponsor diagnosis
unitMap.practicalWork: Learner fieldwork must gather lawful organization/customer evidence, construct the baseline and evidence pack, and integrate evidence across functions.

unitMap.text: Phase 3 (Weeks 9–14): generate alternatives, test a prototype or process change, and update a risk register.
viewingSequence: Begin with L08–L12 for project selection and multi-criteria comparison. Lecture IDs: MBA114-L08, MBA114-L09, MBA114-L10, MBA114-L11, MBA114-L12

Then L19–L28 for risk, quantitative analysis, decision trees, and abandonment. Lecture IDs: MBA114-L19, MBA114-L20, MBA114-L21, MBA114-L22, MBA114-L23, MBA114-L24, MBA114-L25, MBA114-L26, MBA114-L27, MBA114-L28
Finish with L55–L58 for quality and Six Sigma improvement tools. Lecture IDs: MBA114-L55, MBA114-L56, MBA114-L57, MBA114-L58
coveredTopics: project selection and multi-criteria decision analysis (L08–L12)
risk identification, controls, standalone risk analysis and Hillier/simulation analysis (L19–L25)
quality management and Six Sigma / variability tools (L55–L58)
uncoveredTopics: designing and testing a prototype, pilot or process-change experiment with real users/operations
iterative learning loops and updating the risk register from observed test results
evidence-to-alternative synthesis for this particular sponsor problem
unitMap.practicalWork: Viewing is not experimentation: learner must generate locally relevant alternatives, run an ethical prototype/pilot or process test, and update the risk register from results.

unitMap.text: Phase 4 (Weeks 15–20): build implementation, resource, governance, and change-management plan.
viewingSequence: Begin with L04–L05 for PMO and stakeholder concepts. Lecture IDs: MBA114-L04, MBA114-L05
Then L31–L32 for teams, conflict, negotiation, and HR/time issues. Lecture IDs: MBA114-L31, MBA114-L32

Work through L33–L51 for scheduling, PERT/CPM, uncertainty, floats, and time-cost tradeoffs. Lecture IDs: MBA114-L33, MBA114-L34, MBA114-L35, MBA114-L36, MBA114-L37, MBA114-L38, MBA114-L39, MBA114-L40, MBA114-L41, MBA114-L42, MBA114-L43, MBA114-L44, MBA114-L45, MBA114-L46, MBA114-L47, MBA114-L48, MBA114-L49, MBA114-L50, MBA114-L51
Then L52–L54 for cost management, control, and estimation. Lecture IDs: MBA114-L52, MBA114-L53, MBA114-L54
Finish L59 for procurement management. Lecture IDs: MBA114-L59
coveredTopics: team building, conflict, negotiation and time management (L31–L32)
project scheduling, PERT/CPM, probabilistic networks, slacks/floats and crashing (L33–L51)
cost management, cost control and estimation (L52–L54)
uncoveredTopics: organization-specific governance, decision rights, sponsor cadence and escalation design
change-management strategy and adoption planning for organizational implementation
resource planning beyond the lecture examples and tailoring execution controls to the host project
unitMap.practicalWork: The learner must build and negotiate a feasible implementation/resource/governance/change plan with the sponsor; videos cannot grant organizational authority or execute the change.

unitMap.text: Phase 5 (Weeks 21–24): deliver sponsor presentation, executive memo, artifact handover, and reflective after-action review.
viewingSequence: Revisit L02 for success criteria. Lecture IDs: MBA114-L02
Use L31–L32 for team/negotiation context. Lecture IDs: MBA114-L31, MBA114-L32
Finish with L60 for procurement closeout and project termination. Lecture IDs: MBA114-L60
coveredTopics: project success criteria as a close-out lens (L02)
uncoveredTopics: preparing and delivering the sponsor-facing presentation and executive memo/report
artifact handover, implementation recommendation and sponsor/peer feedback exchange
structured after-action review and personal leadership-impact reflection
unitMap.practicalWork: Sponsor presentation, report, artifact handover, feedback, and reflection are required learner work; no lecture substitutes for delivery or genuine sponsor/peer response.

remainingGaps: Phase 1: Public lectures address PM foundations, organizational structures, PMOs, stakeholders and success, but do not teach securing a real sponsor/decision owner, drafting this course’s sponsor-approved charter, or a complete consent/privacy/data-ethics plan and project-specific success metrics.

Phase 2: Market/demand, financial, technical and plant-capacity topics are taught; project-specific customer discovery, primary research, data-quality controls, operational baseline collection, and cross-functional evidence synthesis remain learner work and are not fully taught in these videos.

Phase 3: Alternatives/selection, quantitative risk analysis and quality tools are covered; there is no verified lecture here that fully teaches designing and running a real prototype/pilot/process-change experiment or using its results in an iterative learning loop and revised risk register.

Phase 4: Team, schedule, cost, procurement and PMO concepts are present; organization-specific governance/decision rights and a complete change-management/adoption plan are not fully covered by the verified lectures.

Phase 5: NPTEL includes project termination and some success/team context, but no verified lecture fully covers sponsor-facing executive reports/presentations, artifact handover, obtaining genuine sponsor/peer feedback, or after-action and leadership-impact reflection.

HBS FIELD faculty sponsorship, cohort/team experience, global immersion, live feedback and company project are inherently experiential and cannot be supplied by public lectures. MIT OCW ESD.36 was checked as an adjacent university source; its course pages expose a calendar/lecture notes/projects rather than verified individual lecture recordings, so it is not counted as a video supplement.

courses.title: Probability, Statistics, and Inference for Finance
courses.level: Undergraduate substitute — MIT 18.650 (not a current MFin degree course).
prerequisites: Single-variable calculus, linear algebra, and basic Python or spreadsheet use.
objectives: Estimate distributions, uncertainty, and sampling error in financial data.
Apply likelihood, hypothesis tests, regression, and Bayesian updating.
Communicate model assumptions, diagnostics, and limitations.
units: Unit 1: probability models, random variables, expectation, and simulation.
Unit 2: parametric inference and maximum likelihood.
Unit 3: moments, tests, goodness-of-fit, and multiple-comparison caution.
Unit 4: regression, PCA, and model validation on a financial return panel.
Unit 5: Bayesian updating and a reproducible inference memo.
courses.assignment: Submit a reproducible notebook using one public financial or macroeconomic dataset: data dictionary, exploratory analysis, one estimator, one hypothesis test, regression diagnostics, and a 1,200-word uncertainty memo.
courses.assessment: Rubric (100): data provenance/reproducibility 25; correct inference 30; diagnostics and assumptions 25; interpretation/limits 20.
courses.mapping: Official core: Financial Mathematics or Advanced Financial Mathematics for Financial Engineering — probability and statistics strand; free MIT undergraduate substitute.

unitMap.text: Unit 4: regression, PCA, and model validation on a financial return panel.

uncoveredTopics: An end-to-end worked example of regression diagnostics and PCA on a financial return panel; the available MIT lectures teach the methods but are not verified finance-panel walkthroughs.
unitMap.practicalWork: The return-panel construction, choice of financial variables, regression diagnostics, PCA interpretation and validation on the chosen data remain learner work. Generic method videos do not replace this practical application.

unitMap.text: Unit 5: Bayesian updating and a reproducible inference memo.
viewingSequence: Lecture 17 introduces Bayesian statistics.
Lecture 18 continues Bayesian statistics; follow both before preparing the inference memo.
unitMap.practicalWork: Write and reproduce the 1,200-word uncertainty memo and notebook analysis yourself; no video is a substitute for the submitted work.

courses.title: Programming for Quantitative Finance
courses.level: Undergraduate substitute — MIT 6.0001; optional pre-bridge: Harvard CS50P.
prerequisites: No prior programming required; complete CS50P Weeks 0–6 if Python is new.
objectives: Write and test Python functions, data structures, and simulations.
Build transparent data-cleaning and pricing workflows.
Use version control, documentation, and unit tests to make analysis auditable.
units: Unit 1: expressions, control flow, functions, and test cases.
Unit 2: lists, dictionaries, files, and parsing market-data CSVs.
Unit 3: classes, exceptions, complexity, and code review.
Unit 4: Monte Carlo simulation and discounted-cash-flow functions.
Unit 5: package a small analytics library with README and tests.
courses.assignment: Build a documented Python package that imports a lawful public CSV, validates fields, computes returns and summary statistics, simulates a simple payoff, and includes at least eight tests.
courses.assessment: Rubric (100): correctness 30; tests/edge cases 25; data handling 20; readability/documentation 15; responsible use and reproducibility 10.

unitMap.text: Unit 1: decision variables, feasible sets, and financial constraints.
viewingSequence: Start with the archived Stanford introduction for the optimization action/variable and objective framing.
Use archived Stanford Lecture 5 to distinguish feasible-set identification from optimality.
Use archived Stanford Lecture 6 for convex quadratic/linear constraints, then MIT Lecture 14 for portfolio-specific constraints.
coveredTopics: Feasibility and feasible-set reasoning in convex optimization.
Linear and quadratic constrained formulations as templates for allocation/capital-rationing models.
Portfolio optimization constraints as a finance application.
uncoveredTopics: A directly worked capital-budgeting/capital-rationing formulation is not verified; the video offers general constrained-program templates and portfolio-constraint theory rather than a capital-allocation case.
unitMap.practicalWork: Instantiate the general formulation in a finance case yourself. The assignment’s hypothetical long-only or capital-rationing model, assumptions and allocation rules remain learner work.

unitMap.text: Unit 2: convex sets, duality intuition, and numerical conditioning.
viewingSequence: Study convex sets and cones in archived Stanford Lecture 2.
Follow with Lagrangian duality in Lecture 8.
Finish with Lectures 13–14 for numerical linear algebra, matrix factorizations and computational complexity.
coveredTopics: Convex sets, cones, polyhedra, PSD cones and operations preserving convexity.
Lagrangian duality, weak/strong duality and Slater condition.
Numerical linear algebra structures, factorization methods and computational-cost considerations.
uncoveredTopics: A direct treatment of numerical conditioning (condition numbers, scaling diagnostics and the effect of ill-conditioning on optimizer outputs) is not verified in the selected recordings.
unitMap.practicalWork: Apply numerical checks to your own solver and report instability; the videos do not validate a finance data matrix or software environment.

unitMap.text: Unit 3: mean-variance allocation and benchmark/turnover constraints.
viewingSequence: Review quadratic programming and robust LP model classes in Stanford Lecture 6.
Watch Stanford Lecture 7 for the risk-return frontier/scalarization perspective.
Watch MIT 18.S096 Lecture 14 for Markowitz mean-variance optimization, portfolio constraints and risk measures.
coveredTopics: Quadratic programming as a constrained optimization model class.
Portfolio constraints and risk measures at the general portfolio-theory level.
uncoveredTopics: Specific benchmark-relative weight constraints and turnover bounds are not explicitly verified in these lectures.
unitMap.practicalWork: Encode the requested benchmark and turnover constraints in your own allocation notebook; neither lecture supplies the assignment’s chosen benchmark or data.

unitMap.text: Unit 4: regularization, robust sensitivity, and transaction-cost approximations.
viewingSequence: Use Lecture 6 for robust linear-programming foundations.
Use Lecture 9 for perturbation and sensitivity analysis.
Use Lecture 10 for regularization, penalty approximations and stochastic/worst-case robust approximation.
coveredTopics: General robust and worst-case approximation frameworks.
uncoveredTopics: Portfolio-specific robust sensitivity examples are not verified in these lectures.
No selected free lecture explicitly models transaction-cost approximations for portfolio rebalancing.
unitMap.practicalWork: Estimate and stress-test transaction-cost assumptions in your own model; generic robust approximation is not a substitute for a finance-specific cost model.

unitMap.text: Unit 5: compare an optimizer with a transparent heuristic and write limits.
viewingSequence: Review optimization formulation and feasibility (Stanford Lectures 1 and 5).
Connect portfolio risk-return trade-offs with sensitivity and robust-model limits (Lectures 7, 9 and 10).
Then perform the heuristic comparison and write the recommendation yourself.
coveredTopics: Optimization formulation, feasibility and model-class reasoning.
Sensitivity and robustness concepts that help frame model limitations.
uncoveredTopics: A transparent portfolio-allocation heuristic versus optimizer comparison is not directly taught in the selected videos.
No lecture substitutes for the required learner-written limitations and nontechnical interpretation.
unitMap.practicalWork: This unit is substantially learner work: implement and compare a transparent heuristic, interpret results, and write model limitations/recommendation as required.

remainingGaps: Unit 1: A directly worked capital-budgeting/capital-rationing formulation is not verified; the video offers general constrained-program templates and portfolio-constraint theory rather than a capital-allocation case.
Unit 2: A direct treatment of numerical conditioning (condition numbers, scaling diagnostics and the effect of ill-conditioning on optimizer outputs) is not verified in the selected recordings.
Unit 3: Specific benchmark-relative weight constraints and turnover bounds are not explicitly verified in these lectures.
Unit 4: Portfolio-specific robust sensitivity examples are not verified in these lectures.
Unit 4: No selected free lecture explicitly models transaction-cost approximations for portfolio rebalancing.
Unit 5: A transparent portfolio-allocation heuristic versus optimizer comparison is not directly taught in the selected videos.
