unitMap.text: Unit 1: research question, data lineage, and return construction.
viewingSequence: IITM-01 → IITM-02: course motivation, empirical questions and the role of data.
IITM-03 → IITM-04: formulating a hypothesis, data collection, model specification and empirical workflow.
MITF-15: factor-model concepts as a finance-specific context for later return/factor panel construction.
coveredTopics: Formulating an empirical research question and hypothesis
Basic econometric workflow from data collection through model estimation
Financial factor-model concepts and factor exposure context
uncoveredTopics: Operational construction of adjusted-price or total-return series, including dividend/split handling and return aggregation
Point-in-time data lineage and documentation of vintage/availability dates
Look-ahead prevention in financial feature construction and target alignment
unitMap.practicalWork: Videos do not build or audit the learner’s dataset. The learner must document source/version/timestamps, implement returns and factor joins, and verify no future information enters the predictors.

unitMap.text: Unit 2: OLS, factor exposure, residual diagnostics, and robust errors.
viewingSequence: IITM-07 → IITM-11: classical linear regression model and assumptions.
IITM-12 → IITM-16: goodness of fit, ANOVA and hypothesis testing.
AE-REG1 → AE-REG2 → AE-REG3 → AE-REG4: short lessons on simple/multiple OLS, interpreting models and collinearity.
MITF-06 → MITF-15: linear-regression foundations followed by finance factor-model families/exposures.
IITM-44 → IITM-55: multicollinearity, autocorrelation and heteroskedasticity assumption-relaxation lessons.
coveredTopics: OLS and multiple linear regression foundations
Model fit, ANOVA, inference and hypothesis testing
Financial factor model types and exposure concepts
Residual-assumption concerns: multicollinearity, autocorrelation and heteroskedasticity
uncoveredTopics: Explicit heteroskedasticity-robust/HAC standard-error estimation and selection are not verified by the lecture descriptions/titles; assumption tests or corrections are not equivalent to a robust-covariance tutorial
unitMap.practicalWork: Estimate in an open tool (for example statsmodels or R), inspect residuals, select and justify covariance assumptions, and reproduce a factor-exposure regression. Video software demonstrations do not replace the code, diagnostics or evidence.

unitMap.text: Unit 3: classification/trees, calibration, and imbalanced outcomes.
viewingSequence: IITM-56 → IITM-65: qualitative-response models, linear probability/logit/probit and related limited-response treatment.
AE-LOGIT → AE-THRESH → AE-ROC: logistic model, probability threshold choices and ROC evaluation.
AE-CART → AE-RF → AE-CV: CART, random forests and cross-validation.
coveredTopics: Threshold selection and ROC-based discrimination evaluation
uncoveredTopics: Probability calibration (reliability/calibration curves or equivalent) is not explicitly taught in the selected recordings
Handling imbalanced financial outcomes (class weighting/resampling, suitable precision-recall metrics and prevalence-aware evaluation) is not explicitly taught
unitMap.practicalWork: The learner must choose thresholds and metrics appropriate to outcome prevalence, test calibration/imbalance, and explain consequences. Watching ROC or classification lessons does not establish satisfactory performance.

unitMap.text: Unit 4: time-series splits, leakage checks, and backtest design.
viewingSequence: IITM-28 → IITM-32: structural-break analysis; IITM-38 → IITM-43: seasonal effects.
IITM-44 → IITM-55: autocorrelation/heteroskedasticity and related time-series diagnostics.
MITF-08 → MITF-11 → MITF-12: finance-oriented time-series sequence, from stationary-process foundations through multivariate series and cointegration/state-space topics.
MITF-09: financial volatility context.
AE-CV: cross-validation overview, used only as a general validation supplement.
coveredTopics: Structural breaks and seasonal effects in regression contexts
Autocorrelation and heteroskedasticity as time-series/model diagnostics
Stationarity, multivariate time-series, cointegration and volatility foundations
uncoveredTopics: Chronological holdout/walk-forward or rolling-origin evaluation for financial forecasts is not directly verified
Financial look-ahead/leakage controls and event-time/availability alignment are not explicitly taught
Backtest design choices and an economic benchmark comparison are not developed as a complete recorded lesson
unitMap.practicalWork: The learner must pre-specify and implement a time-ordered split, prevent target/feature leakage, compare an economic baseline, and document the design. Cross-validation lecture alone is not proof of a valid financial backtest.

unitMap.text: Unit 5: model-risk memo and monitoring plan.
viewingSequence: MITF-07: market-risk/VaR context; MITF-09 → MITF-10: volatility and regularized financial risk models.
MITF-15: factor model risks/context.
IITM-44 → IITM-55: assumption problems that inform model limitations.
AE-BASE: a short lesson on comparison to an expert baseline; then write the learner’s own model-risk memo.
coveredTopics: Volatility and regularized pricing/risk model context
Factor model families and common regression assumption failures
Model-versus-baseline comparison as a communication prompt
uncoveredTopics: A finance predictive-model risk memo with explicit unsupported-use boundaries is not taught as a complete lecture
Operational monitoring, drift/stability thresholds, escalation and remediation plan are not covered by a verified selected recording
Ethical evaluation of analytics and responsible interpretation/use boundaries are not explicitly taught in the selected recordings
unitMap.practicalWork: The assigned research note, diagnostics, baseline comparison, explicit limitations, model-risk memo and monitoring plan remain learner-authored work. Videos cannot substitute for assignment completion or any credential.

remainingGaps: Unit 1 — no selected public lecture fully teaches point-in-time financial dataset lineage, corporate-action-adjusted return construction, and look-ahead-safe target/feature alignment; introductory econometrics workflow and factor-model context are partial support.

Unit 2 — an explicit tutorial on heteroskedasticity-robust/HAC covariance estimation and choosing robust standard errors was not verified; diagnostics and assumption-relaxation are only partial coverage.

Unit 3 — probability calibration and imbalanced-outcome evaluation for financial classifiers remain uncovered by the selected verified lectures; logit, thresholds, ROC, trees and cross-validation are partial coverage.

Unit 4 — no selected public lecture directly covers walk-forward/rolling-origin financial validation, look-ahead/leakage prevention, and complete backtest design with economic baselines; general time-series and cross-validation lessons are partial.

Unit 5 — finance-specific predictive model-risk memo content, an operational monitoring/drift/escalation plan, and explicit ethical evaluation/responsible-use teaching were not found in the selected public lecture set; risk-model context and baseline comparison are partial.

courses.title: Financial Accounting and Statement Analysis
courses.level: Undergraduate/professional substitute — NPTEL/IIT; not MIT graduate credit.
prerequisites: Comfort with algebra; MFIN-102 spreadsheet/Python skills helpful.
objectives: Link income statement, balance sheet, and cash-flow statement.
Analyze revenue, inventory, financing, and working-capital choices.
Identify reporting-quality, control, and governance risks.
units: Unit 1: accounting equation and the three-statement map.
Unit 2: accruals, revenue, inventory, depreciation, and cash flow.
Unit 3: financing, leases, taxes, and ratio analysis.
Unit 4: controls, audit signals, and quality-of-earnings adjustments.
Unit 5: comparative public-company analysis.
courses.assignment: Analyze two annual reports for one listed company: build a three-statement linkage sheet, calculate 12 ratios, make five adjustments/risk observations, and write a 1,200-word credit or investor memo.
courses.assessment: Rubric (100): statement accuracy 35; economic interpretation 30; controls/governance analysis 20; sources/clarity 15.
courses.mapping: Official core: Corporate Financial Accounting; free NPTEL/OpenStax substitute.

unitMap.text: Unit 1: accounting equation and the three-statement map.
viewingSequence: MFIN105-L01 → MFIN105-L02 for purpose and statement overview.
MFIN105-L24 → MFIN105-L03 through MFIN105-L07 for transaction recording and balance-sheet structure.
coveredTopics: accounting purpose and basic accounting concepts
recording financial transactions as the basis for statement construction
relationship of financial statements at introductory level
unitMap.practicalWork: Viewing does not replace practicing the accounting equation, reconciling an actual company’s statements, or building the learner’s own three-statement linkage sheet.

unitMap.text: Unit 2: accruals, revenue, inventory, depreciation, and cash flow.
viewingSequence: MFIN105-L24 for transaction recording, followed by MFIN105-L08 through MFIN105-L10 for profit-and-loss accounting.
MFIN105-L11 → MFIN105-L13 for depreciation and inventory valuation.
MFIN105-L14 → MFIN105-L18 for cash-flow statements.
coveredTopics: accounting transactions and timing foundations relevant to accrual reporting
unitMap.practicalWork: The learner must still trace a chosen issuer’s revenue-recognition judgments, inventory and depreciation policies, and reconcile accrual earnings to cash using its annual reports.

unitMap.text: Unit 3: financing, leases, taxes, and ratio analysis.
viewingSequence: MFIN105-L03 → MFIN105-L07 and MFIN105-L08 → MFIN105-L10 for balance-sheet and income-statement context.
MFIN105-L29 → MFIN105-L31 for financial statement interpretation and ratio analysis.
coveredTopics: balance-sheet financing categories at introductory statement level
uncoveredTopics: lease accounting and the effect of lease classification/recognition on statements and ratios
income-tax accounting, deferred taxes and tax-related statement effects
a focused treatment of financing instruments/accounting beyond general balance-sheet presentation
unitMap.practicalWork: The learner must independently identify lease and tax disclosures and compute comparable ratios across the two selected annual reports; NPTEL lectures do not expressly teach the listed lease/tax subtopics.

unitMap.text: Unit 4: controls, audit signals, and quality-of-earnings adjustments.
viewingSequence: MFIN105-L19 → MFIN105-L21 for governance frameworks and Enron governance failure.
MFIN105-L22 for accounting standards, then MFIN105-L29 → MFIN105-L31 for interpretation and ratio signals.
coveredTopics: corporate governance concepts and global models
Enron governance failure as a reporting-risk case
high-level financial-statement interpretation and ratio-based signals
uncoveredTopics: internal accounting controls and control testing/procedures
audit evidence, audit opinions and specific audit red flags
quality-of-earnings normalization and adjustment methodology (recurring/nonrecurring items, working-capital or EBITDA adjustments)
unitMap.practicalWork: Videos do not replace inspecting filings, testing source evidence, distinguishing auditor assurance from buyer-side quality-of-earnings work, or making and defending the assignment’s five adjustments/risk observations.

unitMap.text: Unit 5: comparative public-company analysis.
viewingSequence: MFIN105-L29 → MFIN105-L31 for an analytical framework and ratios.
MFIN105-L25 → MFIN105-L28 for Zee and Hindalco financial-statement cases.
MFIN105-L32 → MFIN105-L35 for Shipping Corporation of India; MFIN105-L36 → MFIN105-L39 for TCS and RIL comparative company cases.
coveredTopics: interpreting company financial statements using actual public-company cases
balance-sheet, income-statement and cash-flow analysis in case contexts
ratio analysis and financial performance interpretation
comparative analysis across public issuers and industries at an instructional level
unitMap.practicalWork: Case videos are worked examples, not substitutes for the required independent two-annual-report analysis, twelve ratio calculations, five sourced observations/adjustments, or the 1,200-word credit/investor memo.

remainingGaps: Unit 3: no verified public lecture in the checked official NPTEL core series specifically teaches lease accounting, deferred/income-tax accounting, or financing-instrument accounting in depth; general balance-sheet and ratio lectures are only partial context.

Unit 4: no verified public lecture in the checked series covers internal control procedures/testing, audit evidence/opinions, or systematic quality-of-earnings adjustment methodology. Governance and Enron lectures are partial adjacent coverage, not audit/QoE instruction.
Unit 3: lease accounting and the effect of lease classification/recognition on statements and ratios
Unit 3: income-tax accounting, deferred taxes and tax-related statement effects
Unit 3: a focused treatment of financing instruments/accounting beyond general balance-sheet presentation
Unit 4: internal accounting controls and control testing/procedures
Unit 4: audit evidence, audit opinions and specific audit red flags
Unit 4: quality-of-earnings normalization and adjustment methodology (recurring/nonrecurring items, working-capital or EBITDA adjustments)

courses.title: Corporate Finance, Valuation, and Capital Allocation
courses.level: Graduate substitute — MIT 15.401 (archived course; not a current MFin offering).
prerequisites: MFIN-101, MFIN-105, and present-value algebra.
objectives: Value cash flows with discounting, no-arbitrage, and cost-of-capital logic.
Estimate WACC/APV implications and make capital-allocation recommendations.
Explain capital structure, payout, and real-options trade-offs.
units: Unit 1: time value, bond/equity valuation, and discount rates.
Unit 2: free cash flow, WACC, APV, and capital structure.
Unit 3: capital budgeting under uncertainty and real options.
Unit 4: payouts, agency/conflicts, and financing choices.
Unit 5: valuation recommendation and sensitivity defense.
courses.assignment: Submit a 12–15 page valuation and capital-allocation case for a real or hypothetical firm: operating forecast, FCF, WACC/APV, sensitivity/scenario table, financing recommendation, and investment-committee memo.
courses.assessment: Rubric (100): model integrity 30; assumptions/evidence 25; valuation and sensitivity 25; capital-allocation judgment 20.
courses.mapping: Official cores: Foundations of Modern Finance and Corporate Finance; closest open archived MIT graduate-course substitute.

NYUCF25-S10 → NYUCF25-S16 → NYUCF25-S17 → NYUCF25-S18 for cost of debt, debt/equity trade-off and cost-of-capital/WACC optimization.

Adjusted present value (APV) and peer-group financing assessment
Debt design and project/firm financing choices
unitMap.practicalWork: The student must build and audit the actual firm forecast, FCF, WACC/APV calculations, assumptions and recommendation; lecture viewing is not a substitute for spreadsheet/model work.

unitMap.text: Unit 3: capital budgeting under uncertainty and real options.
viewingSequence: MIT401-S17 → MIT401-S18 for NPV, IRR, profitability index and capital rationing.
NYUCF25-S13 → NYUCF25-S14 for uncertain project analysis, incremental cash flows, NPV/IRR comparisons and side costs/benefits.
MIT401-S12 for option-pricing foundations, then NYUCF25-S15 for real options in investment analysis.
coveredTopics: NPV-based capital budgeting, cash-flow estimation, IRR, profitability index and capital rationing
Option-pricing background and real-options treatment in investment analysis

unitMap.text: Unit 4: payouts, agency/conflicts, and financing choices.
viewingSequence: NYUCF25-S03 for managerial/shareholder and stockholder/bondholder conflicts and governance context.
NYUCF25-S16 → NYUCF25-S17 → NYUCF25-S19 → NYUCF25-S20 for financing choice, capital structure, APV and debt design.
NYUCF25-S21 → NYUCF25-S22 → NYUCF25-S23 → NYUCF25-S24 for dividends, cash return and payout policy.
MIT401-S07 supplements priority-of-payout and bondholder-risk mechanics.

unitMap.practicalWork: Learner must decide and justify the financing and payout policy for the chosen firm; lecture examples do not replace the assignment’s judgment.

unitMap.text: Unit 5: valuation recommendation and sensitivity defense.
viewingSequence: MIT401-S03 and MIT401-S16 for NPV and discount-rate foundations.
NYUCF25-S11 → NYUCF25-S13 → NYUCF25-S14 for hurdle rates, uncertain project assumptions and alternative project analyses.
NYUCF25-S17 → NYUCF25-S19 for cost-of-capital/APV financing implications.
NYUCF25-S25 → NYUCF25-S26 for valuation and synthesis.

Project uncertainty, alternative analyses and investment recommendation context

unitMap.text: Unit 1: market structure, return measurement, and benchmarks.
viewingSequence: MIT15-S12 then MIT15-S13 for return distributions, historical risk/return and measurement context.
Y252-L04 and Y252-L07 for portfolio-return and Sharpe-ratio framing; Y252-L06 supplies a concrete manager/market-relative investment comparison.
Y252-L19 then Y252-L21 for financial-market intermediaries, trading venues, brokers/dealers and clearing/settlement institutions.
coveredTopics: Market institutions and exchange/intermediation structure: exchanges, brokers, dealers, clearinghouses, investment banks.
Equity and bond return/risk properties; historical equity premium; mean, dispersion and risk-adjusted (Sharpe) return comparisons.
Benchmark-relative manager outcomes and the limitations of Sharpe comparisons, including illiquid-asset measurement issues.
uncoveredTopics: A worked, methodical treatment of arithmetic versus geometric returns, time-weighted versus money-weighted returns, and the calculations/interpretation of benchmark-relative excess returns.
A formal method for choosing a benchmark matched to portfolio mandate, risk, and investable universe.
unitMap.practicalWork: For the policy-portfolio assignment, choose and justify a benchmark and calculate returns from the supplied/selected data yourself; videos do not generate or validate the submitted series.

unitMap.text: Unit 2: mean-variance portfolios, CAPM, and factor-model evidence.
viewingSequence: Y252-L04 for Markowitz mean-variance, efficient frontier, tangency portfolio and CAPM overview.
MIT15-S14 then MIT15-S15 for portfolio mean/variance, covariance/correlation, tangency portfolio and Sharpe ratio.
MIT15-S16 then MIT15-S17 for CAPM/APT, security-market-line performance evaluation, applications, and cross-sectional sorts.
coveredTopics: Mean-variance portfolio choice, covariance/correlation, efficient frontier, tangency portfolio and Sharpe ratio.
CAPM beta, equilibrium expected returns and security market line; APT/multifactor theory at a lecture level.
Some empirical/model evidence: risk/return patterns and CAPM portfolio sorts by size, beta and volatility.
uncoveredTopics: Full construction and interpretation of modern empirical equity factor models (e.g., Fama-French/Carhart factor definitions, regression design, estimation/testing, and limits of factor evidence) is not developed by the verified videos at sufficient depth.
unitMap.practicalWork: Learner must estimate or otherwise substantiate factor/portfolio exposures with the chosen data and distinguish expected-return claims from implementability and risk; viewing alone is not empirical analysis.

unitMap.text: Unit 3: efficient markets, anomalies, and empirical skepticism.
viewingSequence: Y252-L07 for EMH, tests, random-walk claims, technical analysis and skeptical counterevidence.
MIT15-S18 then MIT15-S19 and MIT15-S20 for formal efficiency framing, behavioral critique/adaptive markets and limits of CAPM.
Y252-L11 for behavioral explanations; MIT15-S13 provides size, value and momentum anomaly examples.
coveredTopics: Efficient-markets hypothesis and implications for public information and price changes.
Testing/empirical skepticism, random walk versus alternative behavior, limits and counterexamples, including active-manager and illiquid-market issues.
Behavioral finance and examples of anomalies (size, value and momentum) and adaptive-markets framing.
unitMap.practicalWork: Learner must appraise evidence quality, selection/data-mining risks and whether any apparent anomaly survives the chosen benchmark, sample, costs and risk controls.

unitMap.text: Unit 4: security analysis, active management, and implementation costs.
viewingSequence: Y252-L09 for corporate equity/security-market context.
Y252-L06 then Y252-L20 for asset allocation, security selection, professional management, fiduciary duties and institutional/active-manager context.
MIT15-S16 and MIT15-S17 for CAPM/SML-based performance comparison and empirical portfolio-sorting illustrations.
coveredTopics: Public equity/security-market context and broad role of security selection.
Active investment management, asset allocation, manager performance comparisons, fiduciary duties and institutional investment constraints.
uncoveredTopics: A systematic, video-taught security-analysis workflow (e.g., security valuation/research process) is not clearly present in the verified lectures; MIT 15.433 Investments provides notes but not course videos.
Implementation frictions are not modeled in sufficient detail: explicit/implicit transaction costs, spreads/market impact, turnover, liquidity/capacity, and net-of-cost active performance.
unitMap.practicalWork: Learner still selects securities/weights and estimates feasible costs using current data. Do not treat historic endowment performance examples as evidence that a proposed strategy is investable.

unitMap.text: Unit 5: portfolio policy statement and attribution.
viewingSequence: Y252-L20 for fiduciary duties, institutional investors, endowments and policy context.
Y252-L06 for asset allocation, market timing, security selection and real-world portfolio/manager comparison.
Y252-L07 followed by MIT15-S16 for Sharpe and security-market-line approaches to evaluating performance.
coveredTopics: Institutional-investor governance/fiduciary context and long-horizon asset allocation.
Manager/portfolio performance comparison, Sharpe ratio caveats, and CAPM/SML evaluation concepts.
uncoveredTopics: A complete return-attribution procedure (e.g., factor attribution or allocation/selection decomposition) with calculation and interpretation is not taught sufficiently for the assignment.
unitMap.practicalWork: The policy statement, benchmark choice, return/factor attribution, evidence review, rebalancing rule and one-page client-style risk disclosure remain learner-created deliverables; the 100-point original rubric remains unchanged (theory-to-design fit 25; calculations 30; benchmark/attribution 20; costs/risks 15; clarity 10).

remainingGaps: Unit 1 — Quantitative return measurement (arithmetic/geometric and time-/money-weighted forms), benchmark-matched excess-return calculations, and a formal benchmark-selection method: best verified partial coverage is MIT15-S12/S13 plus Yale ECON 252 Lectures 4, 6 and 7.

Unit 2 — Detailed modern empirical equity-factor construction and econometric evidence (including Fama-French/Carhart factor definitions, estimation, testing and limitations): best verified partial coverage is MIT 15.401 Sessions 13, 15 and 17 and Yale Lecture 4.

Unit 4 — Systematic security-analysis workflow and quantitative implementation-cost analysis (explicit/implicit trading costs, spread/impact, turnover, liquidity/capacity and net-of-cost active returns): best verified partial coverage is Yale Lectures 6, 9 and 20 plus MIT Session 16.

Unit 5 — A calculation-ready portfolio return-attribution method (factor attribution or allocation/selection decomposition): best verified partial coverage is MIT Session 16 (SML evaluation) and Yale Lectures 6, 7 and 20.

lectures.provider: MIT OpenCourseWare, 18.642 Topics in Mathematics with Applications in Finance, Fall 2024
lectures.coverageNote: Supplementary official MIT segment, not a complete course lecture. The resource description covers compounding, discounting, zero- and coupon-bond pricing, price/yield inverse relation, yield curves, duration and convexity.

lectures.title: Lecture 23: Quanto Credit Hedging
lectures.provider: MIT OpenCourseWare, 18.S096 Topics in Mathematics with Applications in Finance, Fall 2013
lectures.coverageNote: Supplementary MIT guest lecture on quanto credit hedging and use of mathematical models in trading; it is not comprehensive instruction on CDS mechanics or credit-spread valuation.

unitMap.text: Unit 1: cash-flow conventions, price/yield, and spot/forward rates.
viewingSequence: Watch FI-I for coupon-bond cash flows and valuation examples.
Watch FI-II for spot and forward rates, yield curves, forecasts and term-structure models.
Use BOND-MATH as a reinforcement segment on compounding, discounting, zero/coupon bonds and price-yield relations.
coveredTopics: Inverse relation between bond price and yield
Spot rates, forward rates, yield curves and term-structure context
uncoveredTopics: Settlement and accrued-interest conventions
Day-count bases, coupon-frequency conventions, and irregular/stub-period cash flows
unitMap.practicalWork: For the workbook, the learner must specify consistent cash-flow dates and conventions; recordings do not replace calculating and validating the assigned bond cash flows.

unitMap.text: Unit 2: duration, convexity, key-rate exposure, and curve scenarios.
viewingSequence: Begin with BOND-MATH for duration, convexity and bond-price sensitivity concepts.
Watch FI-III for interest-rate-risk measurement in fixed-income valuation.
Use FI-II to connect rate sensitivity to yield curves and term structure.
coveredTopics: Duration and convexity as bond-price sensitivity measures
Yield-curve and term-structure context for rate risk
uncoveredTopics: Key-rate duration/exposure decomposition across curve tenors
Systematic construction and interpretation of parallel and nonparallel curve scenarios and portfolio P&L
unitMap.practicalWork: The required workbook's three curve-shock scenarios and exposure calculations remain learner-built and validated tasks; video viewing does not perform them.

unitMap.text: Unit 3: credit spreads, default/recovery, and credit derivatives.
viewingSequence: Watch FI-IV for corporate-bond risk, payout priority, expected-value and correlation examples.
Watch CREDIT-HEDGE for a specialized mathematical example of quanto credit hedging.
coveredTopics: Sources of risk in corporate bonds
Effect of payout priority and correlation on expected values and bond pricing
uncoveredTopics: Credit-spread measurement, decomposition and shock valuation
Explicit default-probability and recovery-assumption valuation methods
Credit-default-swap contract cash flows and pricing mechanics
unitMap.practicalWork: The assigned credit-spread shock and hedge proposal must be implemented and reasoned through by the learner; these recordings provide only selected background.

unitMap.text: Unit 4: immunization, hedging, liquidity, and model risk.
viewingSequence: Review BOND-MATH for duration/convexity foundations.
Watch FI-III for interest-rate-risk measurement and FI-IV for corporate-bond risk context.
Finish with CREDIT-HEDGE for a specialized credit-hedging example.
coveredTopics: Duration/convexity foundations relevant to rate-risk management
uncoveredTopics: Immunization strategy and rebalancing as a verified video lesson (MIT's 15.401 recitation resource is slides, not video)
Liquidity-risk measurement and liquidity stress
Model-risk and basis-risk identification, quantification and communication
unitMap.practicalWork: The learner must develop the hedge proposal, assess residual basis/model risk, apply risk limits and write the memo; neither videos nor the MIT recitation slides substitute for these tasks.

remainingGaps: Unit 1: verified recordings do not explicitly teach settlement, accrued-interest, day-count, coupon-frequency or stub-period cash-flow conventions.
Unit 2: no verified video explicitly teaches key-rate exposure decomposition or systematic portfolio curve-scenario construction and P&L analysis.

Unit 3: no verified video comprehensively covers credit-spread measurement/decomposition, explicit default/recovery valuation, and CDS mechanics/pricing; MIT 15.401 Part IV covers selected corporate-bond risk and payout priority, while 18.S096 Lecture 23 is a specialized hedge example.
Unit 4: immunization appears in the MIT 15.401 fixed-income recitation slides but those slides are not a video; no verified recordings fully cover liquidity risk or model/basis risk analysis.

unitMap.text: Unit 1: arbitrage, forwards, futures, carry, and margin.
viewingSequence: NPTEL 1–4: derivative basics, forwards, no-arbitrage pricing and consumption-asset carry.
NPTEL 5–7: futures, margin/MTM and exposure; MIT Forward/Futures I–II reinforce contract and pricing examples.
coveredTopics: Forward/futures prices, exposures, payoff and pricing examples
unitMap.practicalWork: Build and test your own payoff and hedge diagrams; lecture examples do not replace the workbook.

unitMap.text: Unit 2: swaps and interest-rate hedging.
viewingSequence: NPTEL 19–22: spot rates/yields, interest-rate risk, duration, price sensitivity and immunization.
NPTEL 23–29: interest-rate/T-bill/T-bond futures, applications, pricing and hedging.
NPTEL 54–58: swaps, FRAs, swap valuation, currency swaps and VaR introduction.
coveredTopics: Spot interest rates, YTM and other yield measures
Interest-rate risk, duration, price sensitivities and immunization
Interest-rate swap valuation and currency swaps
unitMap.practicalWork: Perform the issuer/portfolio interest-rate calculations and workbook documentation yourself.

unitMap.text: Unit 3: option payoff diagrams, binomial replication, and Greeks.
viewingSequence: NPTEL 30–33: options, put-call parity, bounds and American-option properties.
NPTEL 34–36 and MIT Options II: payoff diagrams, strategies and spreads.
NPTEL 44–45 and MIT Options III: binomial valuation/replication.
NPTEL 49–54: Greeks and their use in hedging/trading strategies.
coveredTopics: Put-call parity, price bounds and American options
Option payoff diagrams, strategies and spreads
Binomial pricing and replication / risk-neutral logic
Greeks, sensitivities and use in hedging/trading
unitMap.practicalWork: Draw, calculate and test payoff/hedge diagrams and hedge ratios; viewing cannot substitute for those calculations.

unitMap.text: Unit 4: risk-neutral valuation assumptions, volatility, and implementation limits.
viewingSequence: NPTEL 37–43: random walks, Brownian motion, diffusion, Ito calculus and lognormal distributions.
NPTEL 44–48 and MIT 18.S096 Lecture 19: binomial risk-neutral valuation, Black–Scholes formula and model features.
NPTEL 49: link between Black–Scholes PDE and Greeks.
coveredTopics: Random walk/Brownian motion and diffusion foundations
Central-limit and stochastic calculus topics including Ito
Binomial option pricing and risk-neutral valuation
uncoveredTopics: Practical volatility calibration/validation and implementation limits beyond model features (including volatility smiles/surfaces, stochastic volatility/jumps, and empirical market-model fit) are not comprehensively covered.
unitMap.practicalWork: Learner must select and defend assumptions, run sensitivity/stress tests, and disclose implementation/model limits.

unitMap.text: Unit 5: hedge effectiveness and counterparty/liquidity controls.
viewingSequence: NPTEL 8–12 and 16–18: exposure, futures hedge design/sizing, examples and index futures hedging.
NPTEL 21–29: rate risk, immunization and futures hedging; NPTEL 50–54: Greeks in strategies.
NPTEL 58–60: VaR and bond/derivatives portfolio risk computation.
MIT Forward/Futures I: qualitative illiquidity and counterparty risk context.
coveredTopics: Hedge design, contract count, examples and index futures hedging
VaR for bond and derivative portfolios
uncoveredTopics: Dedicated basis-risk quantification and hedge-effectiveness testing framework
Counterparty collateral, netting, exposure limits and close-out risk controls
Liquidity limits, liquidation stress and mitigation methods
unitMap.practicalWork: Stress tests, hedge effectiveness, counterparty terms, liquidity controls and governance memo are required learner work, not video replacements.

remainingGaps: Unit 4: Matched free lectures do not fully teach practical volatility-surface calibration, empirical model validation, or testing implementation limits (smiles/surfaces, stochastic volatility/jumps, model fit); NPTEL stochastic-process/Black–Scholes and MIT risk-neutral lectures are partial foundations.

Unit 5: No matched public lecture fully covers basis-risk/hedge-effectiveness testing or implementation-grade counterparty collateral/netting/limits and liquidity-control frameworks; NPTEL hedge/VaR and MIT forward/futures risk discussion are partial.

Unit 4: Practical volatility calibration/validation and implementation limits beyond model features (including volatility smiles/surfaces, stochastic volatility/jumps, and empirical market-model fit) are not comprehensively covered.
Unit 5: Dedicated basis-risk quantification and hedge-effectiveness testing framework
Unit 5: Counterparty collateral, netting, exposure limits and close-out risk controls
Unit 5: Liquidity limits, liquidation stress and mitigation methods

courses.title: Market, Credit, and Liquidity Risk Management
courses.level: External professional substitute; not a regulatory qualification.
prerequisites: MFIN-101, MFIN-107, MFIN-108, and MFIN-109.
objectives: Measure market and credit risk with transparent assumptions.
Design stress tests, limits, escalation, and reporting.
Recognize what VaR-like measures miss, including liquidity and model risk.
units: Unit 1: risk taxonomy, returns, exposures, and data quality.
Unit 2: VaR/expected shortfall concepts and backtesting.
Unit 3: scenario analysis, reverse stress, and liquidity horizons.
Unit 4: credit migration/default and concentration risk.
Unit 5: limits, model governance, and board reporting.
courses.assignment: Prepare a risk pack for a hypothetical multi-asset portfolio: exposure inventory, risk metrics, three stresses, breach/escalation rule, model-risk register, and a five-minute risk-committee briefing.
courses.assessment: Rubric (100): measurements and assumptions 30; stress design 25; governance/escalation 25; clarity/actionability 20.
courses.mapping: Official core/elective theme: Foundations of Modern Finance, Analytics of Finance, and Financial Engineering — risk-management strand; free substitute.

unitMap.text: Unit 1: risk taxonomy, returns, exposures, and data quality.
viewingSequence: Start with NPTEL-01, NPTEL-08 and NPTEL-09 for instruments, exposure and the meaning of risk.
Then use NPTEL-13 to NPTEL-16 for portfolio examples and systematic/unsystematic risk.
Finish with CAROL-01 to CAROL-03 for instruments, P&L/returns and portfolio volatility.
uncoveredTopics: a complete enterprise risk taxonomy spanning market, credit, liquidity, operational and model risks
data lineage, missing/stale data, outliers, pricing-source controls and other data-quality diagnostics
unitMap.practicalWork: Do not substitute a portfolio exposure inventory, return-data inspection or source-quality checks with viewing.

unitMap.text: Unit 2: VaR/expected shortfall concepts and backtesting.
viewingSequence: Use NPTEL-58 to NPTEL-60 in series order for VaR definitions and bond/derivative-portfolio computation.
Compare with CAROL-04 to CAROL-06 for definitions and model choices, then watch MIT-01 for an applied institutional market-risk view.
Finish with CAROL-10 for statistical backtesting.
coveredTopics: VaR estimation choices and model comparison
uncoveredTopics: expected shortfall (ES) definition, computation and comparison with VaR
backtesting exception tests and interpretation in context are only partially introduced; no detailed model-specific validation protocol
unitMap.practicalWork: Risk-metric selection, calculations and backtest interpretation in the assignment remain learner work.

unitMap.text: Unit 3: scenario analysis, reverse stress, and liquidity horizons.
viewingSequence: Use NPTEL-58 to NPTEL-60 for risk measures and bond/derivative portfolio calculations.
Watch CAROL-07 for time-horizon scaling (a proxy for understanding horizon assumptions, not liquidity-adjusted VaR).
Then view CAROL-11 and YALE-01 for scenario/stress design, including crisis narratives and a short-term funding-liquidity shock.
coveredTopics: market risk measurement as backdrop for scenarios
scenario analysis and portfolio stress testing
illustrative macro/market stresses, including a short-term liquidity-crisis scenario
uncoveredTopics: reverse stress testing from failure/breach outcomes backward to scenarios
explicit liquidity horizons, liquidation periods, market-depth/funding-liquidity measures and liquidity-adjusted VaR
operational design of scenario calibration and escalation
unitMap.practicalWork: The three portfolio stresses and reverse-stress case must be created and defended by the learner; videos do not generate or validate the assignment scenarios.

unitMap.text: Unit 4: credit migration/default and concentration risk.
viewingSequence: Use NPTEL-22 and NPTEL-23 for rate-risk and bond sensitivity context; NPTEL-29 and NPTEL-30 show government-bond futures exposures, not credit migration.
Use CAROL-08 for spread/rating/credit-VaR basics.
Follow with UOFT-02 and UOFT-03 for introductory and model-based credit-risk lectures, then MIT-02 for counterparty credit risk and credit valuation.
coveredTopics: credit spreads, ratings as risk signals, credit VaR
fixed-income interest-rate sensitivity distinct from borrower default risk
uncoveredTopics: explicit rating-migration transition matrices and migration/default frequency estimation
portfolio concentration risk and sector/name concentration aggregation
a complete default loss decomposition (exposure at default, probability of default, loss given default) and validation are not established by the verified titles/descriptions
unitMap.practicalWork: The learner must define concentrations and exposure assumptions for the hypothetical portfolio; video viewing does not produce the exposure inventory.

unitMap.text: Unit 5: limits, model governance, and board reporting.
viewingSequence: Use UOFT-01 and NPTEL-09 as broad risk-management/exposure context.
Watch CAROL-09 for internal model validation and CAROL-10 for backtesting; CAROL-11 and YALE-01 provide governance-related stress-testing context.

viewingSequence: 1. [Y01] set finance’s professional and social purpose.
2. [Y11] examine moral judgment, integrity, and exploitation risks in financial conduct.

4. [Y20] study investment-manager fiduciary duty and the prudent-person rule.

unitMap.practicalWork: Apply the ethical framework yourself in the assigned decision memo; videos do not replace stakeholder mapping, alternatives, disclosure drafting, escalation-owner selection, or reflective judgment.

unitMap.text: Unit 2: market integrity, information use, and fairness.
viewingSequence: 1. [Y07] begin with the efficient-markets hypothesis and its treatment of public information and performance manipulation.
2. [Y12] study insider-information trading, price manipulation, market surveillance, and layers of regulation.
3. [Y21] finish with exchanges, brokers/dealers, electronic/high-frequency trading, and fairness between private investors and intermediaries.
coveredTopics: How public information enters prices and the empirical limits of the efficient-markets hypothesis (Y07).
Insider information, stock-price manipulation, market surveillance, and regulatory responses (Y12).
Market fairness, brokers versus dealers, exchange structure, electronic/high-frequency trading and flash-crash context (Y21).
unitMap.practicalWork: Learners must still apply the concepts to the hypothetical product/trading model and make their own evidence-based fairness and market-integrity judgment.

coveredTopics: Firm and board accountability, duties of care/loyalty, and multiple levels of financial regulation (Y12).
Board-level governance of technology and data risks, including AI fairness/bias, data privacy, and cybersecurity (CAM02).
AI opacity/autonomy, ex-ante testing constraints, model drift, model-risk-management limitations, and systemic risk (CAM03).

courses.level: Graduate-style integrative capstone with external/archived MIT learning materials.
prerequisites: Completion of MFIN-101 through MFIN-112 or mentor-approved equivalent.
objectives: Frame a decision-relevant finance question and define success/risk limits.

Deliver reproducible analysis and a defensible recommendation to a nontechnical audience.
units: Unit 1: proposal, sponsor/mentor check, data rights, and risk register.
Unit 2: exploratory data/model baseline and literature/resource audit.
Unit 3: core analysis, validation, and economic/financial interpretation.
Unit 4: stress testing, ethics/regulation review, and implementation design.
Unit 5: final report, code handoff, presentation, feedback, and reflection.
courses.assignment: Complete a sponsor-facing 15–20 page report, reproducible code/model annex, data/provenance sheet, risk-and-ethics review, 10-minute presentation, and feedback log. Acceptable topics include valuation/capital allocation, portfolio/risk analytics, fixed-income/derivatives hedge design, or fintech product risk; it must be educational and must not solicit or execute investment transactions.
courses.assessment: Rubric (100): question and evidence 15; quantitative/model quality 25; validation and limitations 20; finance/risk/regulatory integration 20; communication/reproducibility 20.

unitMap.text: Unit 3: core analysis, validation, and economic/financial interpretation.
viewingSequence: FT03 — finance AI application context, if relevant to the chosen question.
RR01 then RR02 — statistical/empirical return properties and financial risk measures.

coveredTopics: AI use cases in finance (conceptual and sector context)
Statistical background and empirical properties/patterns of stock and bond returns
Value-at-Risk models and institutional market-risk management
Credit/lending and trading/capital-market context when relevant to the selected project.

Valuation and capital-allocation methods
Constructing and validating a fixed-income or derivatives hedge
Economic interpretation and limitations specific to the selected dataset and question
Reproducible analysis/code handoff
unitMap.practicalWork: Use only the topic-matched lectures; the project analysis, validation, interpretation, and reproducible annex remain learner work. The VaR lecture is a targeted risk supplement, not a general validation course.

unitMap.text: Unit 4: stress testing, ethics/regulation review, and implementation design.
viewingSequence: FT01 — financial-services technology context.
FT11 — historical financial-crisis context as a prompt for shock thinking.
VAR01 — market-risk measurement and institutional VaR use.
FT07 or FT09 — use the credit or capital-markets sector lecture as appropriate to the intended deployment.
coveredTopics: Financial market-risk measures and institutional VaR application
Credit/lending or capital-market setting for appropriately scoped project risks
uncoveredTopics: Formal scenario-based stress-test design, calibration, and interpretation
Project-specific ethics, privacy, fairness, conflicts, and consumer-protection review
A systematic legal/regulatory compliance analysis for the chosen activity and jurisdiction
Model governance, monitoring, ownership, and controls
Implementation planning, operational controls, and deployment evaluation
unitMap.practicalWork: Videos provide analytical and sector context, not legal advice, an ethics sign-off, or implementation approval. The learner must complete the required risk-and-ethics/regulation review; do not execute transactions.

unitMap.text: Unit 5: final report, code handoff, presentation, feedback, and reflection.
uncoveredTopics: Preparing the required sponsor-facing 15–20 page report
Packaging reproducible code/model annex and data/provenance sheet

No verified free public lecture in the checked series directly teaches this deliverable workflow; learners must produce the artifacts and gather feedback themselves. The course-conclusion lecture is not treated as coverage.

courses.title: Technology Strategy, Foresight, and Roadmapping
courses.level: Graduate-style technology-strategy extension using a full IIT strategic-management lecture foundation plus MIT graduate roadmapping readings.
courses.prerequisites: None beyond work familiarity with one product, platform, or business unit. Bring a real organizational challenge for the capstone.
objectives: Separate technology, product, application, and business strategy in a technology transformation.
Identify external disruption signals, internal capabilities, and measurable figures of merit.
Build a technology roadmap with decision gates, dependencies, and leading indicators.
Turn a transformation narrative into operating experiments and management reviews.
Defend portfolio choices against strategic alternatives.
units: Frame the technology-to-product-to-application-to-business chain and select the capstone organization.
Map external forces, customer segments, and disruption signals; write a two-page situation brief.
Diagnose internal capabilities, culture, and organizational constraints.
Build a three-horizon technology roadmap with figures of merit and decision gates.
Design market experiments, reviews, and metrics that operationalize the roadmap.
Present a portfolio choice and transformation narrative to a mock executive committee.
courses.assignment: Produce a 6–8 page technology roadmap and investment thesis: strategic intent, assumptions, customer/application segments, three horizons, capability dependencies, KPIs, experiment plan, and stop/scale criteria.
courses.assessment: Use the stated rubric: analytical correctness and evidence 30%; application to the chosen organization 30%; decisions, trade-offs, and risk treatment 25%; clarity and executive communication 15%. A score of 80/100 is the self-study passing threshold.

courses.level: Graduate core technical module. MIT 6.824 is a graduate distributed-systems subject. It is not a cloud-vendor certification.

objectives: Explain failure, replication, coordination, and consistency trade-offs to non-specialist executives.
Assess service boundaries, data ownership, and state-management risks in a distributed architecture.

lectures.title: Amy Edmondson | How leaders nurture psychological safety
lectures.provider: Let Go & Lead with Maril MacDonald; interview with Amy C. Edmondson, Harvard Business School Professor
lectures.coverageNote: Public 44:54 full expert interview, not an official Harvard lecture. Covers candor, psychological safety, learning organizations, modern teams, leader behaviors, and learning from failure; see the HBS evidence page for the research-grounded topic framing.

unitMap.text: Reflect on a pivotal technology leadership episode and identify assumptions and stakeholders.
viewingSequence: Use the introductory OB sequence first, then perception, communication, and leadership/power. Bring a real technology-leadership episode and annotate assumptions and affected stakeholders while watching.
coveredTopics: Individual and organizational-behavior lenses for examining a pivotal leadership episode
Perception and interpretation as sources of assumptions
Power, leadership, and influence among stakeholders
Communication as a way to surface perspectives
uncoveredTopics: No academic-video gap for the named learning lens; the learner must supply and analyze a real episode.
unitMap.practicalWork: Select an actual pivotal technology-leadership episode; identify personal assumptions and stakeholders from observation. Viewing supplies analytical lenses, not the learner’s evidence.

unitMap.text: Study leadership styles, following, and distributed leadership; map decision rights.
viewingSequence: Watch the NPTEL power-and-leadership block, then decision-making and structure; finish with the short MIT Leadership Center discussion. Apply the ideas by mapping the organization’s actual decision rights.
coveredTopics: Leadership styles and the relationship between power, leaders, and followers
Distributed leadership, decision autonomy, alignment guardrails, and decision transparency
unitMap.practicalWork: Decision-rights mapping is an applied analysis of the learner’s organization; videos explain the concepts but cannot determine local authority or accountability.

unitMap.text: Assess culture, psychological safety, incentives, and talent-system effects on delivery.
viewingSequence: Begin with NPTEL Learning, Attitudes, Emotions, Motivation, Interpersonal Relationships, and Communication in their course order; continue with Group Dynamics and Organizational Culture; then view the psychological-safety expert interview followed by the selected performance-management lectures on employee development, team performance, appraisal, HR data, rewards, and culture-performance fit.
coveredTopics: Attitudes, emotions, interpersonal relationships, group dynamics, and communication relevant to team delivery
Psychological safety, candor, learning behavior, and leader responses
Talent-system mechanisms: employee development, key performance areas, team performance, 360-degree appraisal, HR decisions, and rewards
unitMap.practicalWork: Assess the organization’s culture, psychological safety, incentives, and talent-system effects using local evidence; video concepts do not replace organizational diagnosis.

unitMap.text: Construct a change narrative, stakeholder map, communications cadence, and resistance plan.
viewingSequence: Watch the seven change-course lectures in NPTEL course order. Then use the primary-series communication and leadership lectures to reinforce the organizational behavior context. Create the case-specific narrative, stakeholder map, communications cadence, resistance plan, and feedback metrics yourself.
coveredTopics: Diagnosing readiness and resistance, including affective, cognitive, behavioral, power, capability, and uncertainty concerns
Selecting implementation approaches and involving stakeholders
Constructing a meaningful change vision and linking it to mission
Communication cadence, participation, sustaining change, and evaluation/feedback
unitMap.practicalWork: The transformation case, stakeholder map, narrative, communications cadence, resistance plan, and feedback metrics must be created for the selected organization.

unitMap.text: Select and view six long-form university leadership lectures; write evidence-based reflections rather than summary notes.
viewingSequence: The required six long-form university lectures are the five primary-series Power and Leadership parts followed by the full-length IIT Kharagpur “Vision and Change” lecture. The MIT Leadership Center short video is an optional post-sequence supplement. Write evidence-based reflections, not viewing summaries.
coveredTopics: Vision as a basis for organizational change
Distributed leadership and its practical implications
unitMap.practicalWork: View six long-form university lectures and write evidence-based reflections. The viewing activity is not a substitute for the reflections or the final transformation plan.

unitMap.text: Run a two-week leadership experiment and record behavior, signals, results, and next adjustment.
viewingSequence: View the listed learning, motivation, leadership, decision, evaluation, and safety content before designing the experiment. Running the two-week experiment, keeping an evidence log, interpreting before/after signals, and choosing the next adjustment are learner fieldwork, not video substitutes.
coveredTopics: Motivation, leadership, decision, and feedback concepts that can inform an experiment
Signals and evaluation approaches for checking outcomes
Psychological safety as an enabling condition for candid feedback
unitMap.practicalWork: Run the specified two-week leadership experiment and record behavior, signals, results, and next adjustment. This is fieldwork, not a video task.

remainingGaps: Unit 1: No academic-video gap for the named learning lens; the learner must supply and analyze a real episode.

courses.title: Technology Operations, Supply Networks, and Service Delivery
courses.level: Graduate core. MIT 15.760B supplies the operations-management framework. MIT ESD.290 is used as the distinct full graduate supply-chain video series; it is broader operations content, not a substitute claim for a full 15.760B video record.
courses.prerequisites: Basic algebra and comfort with measures such as throughput, cycle time, utilization, service level, and cost. CTO-02 architecture package is recommended.
objectives: Map a value stream from demand signal through delivery, operation, and support.
Use capacity, queueing, inventory, quality, and supply-chain concepts to expose bottlenecks.
Tie platform reliability and SRE-style operational measures to customer and economic outcomes.
Select operating KPIs, service-level objectives, and escalation mechanisms.
Make trade-offs among speed, quality, resilience, security, working capital, and sustainability.
units: Draw a current-state product/service value stream and define demand, flow, quality, and reliability measures.
Analyze capacity, queues, bottlenecks, and SLO error-budget implications.
Analyze inventory, procurement, and supplier/third-party concentration risks.
Use production control and quality tools to build operational dashboards and response thresholds.
Study supply-network design and product-development handoffs; set make/buy/platform criteria.
Run an operational review simulation: incident, capacity spike, supplier disruption, and executive decision log.
courses.assignment: Produce a 6–8 page technology operations plan: value-stream map, bottleneck analysis, SLOs/KPIs, capacity and vendor risks, quality controls, incident cadence, and a 90-day improvement backlog with owner and expected effect.
courses.assessment: Use the stated rubric: analytical correctness and evidence 30%; application to the chosen organization 30%; decisions, trade-offs, and risk treatment 25%; clarity and executive communication 15%. A score of 80/100 is the self-study passing threshold.
mapping: Strategic execution and performance tracking
Technology roadmaps with clear performance targets
Operationalizing technology-driven transformation

unitMap.text: Draw a current-state product/service value stream and define demand, flow, quality, and reliability measures.
viewingSequence: NPTEL-01 then NPTEL-35 for operations/supply-chain scope and terminology.
IITR-41 for procurement-to-shipment flow and planned-versus-actual production control.
MIT-01 and MIT-12 for IoT/RFID visibility examples; treat these as technology examples, not a value-stream mapping tutorial.
IITR-49 for quality-control measures, then GOOGLE-SLO for user-facing reliability indicators and objectives.
coveredTopics: Operations and supply-chain flow from procurement through shipment at a high level (IITR-41).
RFID/IoT as sources of product and operational visibility (MIT-01; MIT-12).
Statistical process-quality measurement and reliability indicators (IITR-49; GOOGLE-SLO).
uncoveredTopics: A complete current-state value-stream mapping method for identifying activity, queue/wait, lead time, and information flow across a product or service.
Service-process-specific flow design and a full set of demand/throughput/cycle-time/quality/reliability metric definitions in one matched lecture.
unitMap.practicalWork: Learner must select an organization/service, collect or make defensible estimates for its actual demand and process data, and draw the current-state map; videos do not provide the organization-specific map.

unitMap.text: Analyze capacity, queues, bottlenecks, and SLO error-budget implications.
viewingSequence: NPTEL-08 for demand and capacity planning.
NPTEL-24 then NPTEL-28 for scheduling objectives, job-shop/Gantt representation, and dispatch rules.
NPTEL-30 for shifting bottlenecks and line balancing.
GOOGLE-SLO for measuring reliability and setting a customer-oriented objective.
coveredTopics: Demand and capacity planning and trade-offs (NPTEL-08).
Scheduling/dispatch concepts used to expose constraints in production flow (NPTEL-24; NPTEL-28).
SLI/SLO definitions and reliability target setting (GOOGLE-SLO).
uncoveredTopics: Queueing theory and quantitative waiting-time/variability analysis for service queues.
SLO error-budget policy and explicit trade-offs between reliability targets, release speed, and operational risk.
unitMap.practicalWork: Apply calculations to the chosen organization and set capacity thresholds; select an SLO and decision thresholds using local customer/economic evidence.

unitMap.text: Analyze inventory, procurement, and supplier/third-party concentration risks.
viewingSequence: NPTEL-09 then NPTEL-14 and NPTEL-16 for inventory models, replenishment, lot scheduling, and supply-chain inventory.
NPTEL-20 and NPTEL-21 for safety stock/reorder levels under discrete and normal lead-time demand; NPTEL-23 for delayed differentiation/substitution.
MIT-06 for counterfeit and time/temperature pedigree risk.
MIT-12 then MIT-13 for RFID visibility, transport, adoption, and supply-chain collaboration examples.
coveredTopics: Inventory cost, EOQ, multi-item/production-consumption inventory, and supply-chain inventory (NPTEL-09; NPTEL-14; NPTEL-16).
Safety stock/reorder levels, lead-time demand, and delayed differentiation (NPTEL-20; NPTEL-21; NPTEL-23).
Traceability, counterfeit/product-integrity exposure, and time/temperature pedigree (MIT-06).
RFID implementation, supplier/retailer coordination, and logistics visibility examples (MIT-12; MIT-13).
uncoveredTopics: Quantitative supplier/third-party concentration risk assessment, sourcing and supply-contract choice, and a complete make-or-break risk framework.
Current cloud/service-provider concentration and cyber/operational third-party risk are not covered by the historical RFID and inventory lessons.
unitMap.practicalWork: Learner must identify actual suppliers/dependencies, quantify concentration and substitutability, and document procurement/vendor risks; recordings cannot establish organization-specific exposures.

unitMap.text: Use production control and quality tools to build operational dashboards and response thresholds.
viewingSequence: NPTEL-24, NPTEL-28, and NPTEL-30 for scheduling, Gantt/dispatch control, and bottlenecks.
IITR-41 for production-control functions and progress checks.
IITR-49 for SPC/control charts and statistical quality control.
GOOGLE-SLO for customer-facing reliability indicators/objectives.
coveredTopics: Production scheduling, Gantt charts, dispatch/progress, and planned-versus-actual control (NPTEL-24; NPTEL-28; IITR-41).
SPC, statistical quality control, and control charts (IITR-49).
uncoveredTopics: A technology-operations dashboard that combines customer, service, quality, capacity, and economic indicators with concrete owner/threshold rules.
Operational escalation/incident-cadence design and error-budget thresholds.
unitMap.practicalWork: Learner must select and define organization-specific KPIs, thresholds, owners, escalation paths, and meeting cadence; the videos supply concepts rather than the finished dashboard.

unitMap.text: Study supply-network design and product-development handoffs; set make/buy/platform criteria.
viewingSequence: NPTEL-35 for supply-chain context.
NPTEL-36 then NPTEL-37 and NPTEL-38 for facility/location and transportation/distribution network models.
MIT-08 for automotive RFID research roadmap, lifecycle and design/production feedback; then MIT-13 for an implementation/collaboration case.
NPTEL-41 for the value of information in decisions.
coveredTopics: Supply-chain network location, transportation/distribution, and network design (NPTEL-35; NPTEL-36; NPTEL-37; NPTEL-38).
Product lifecycle management and design/production information handoffs, including lifecycle field feedback (MIT-08).
Supply-chain implementation collaboration and information value (MIT-13; NPTEL-41).
uncoveredTopics: Explicit make-versus-buy, platform/vendor selection, and technology sourcing criteria tied to strategic control, cost, resilience, security, and sustainability.
A contemporary technology-platform roadmap method with measurable target states and options/trade-offs.
unitMap.practicalWork: Learner must build and justify make/buy/platform criteria and apply them to the chosen organization; historical automotive RFID material is a case example, not a reusable decision answer.

unitMap.text: Run an operational review simulation: incident, capacity spike, supplier disruption, and executive decision log.
viewingSequence: NPTEL-08 and NPTEL-30 for capacity and bottleneck decision context.
MIT-06 and MIT-13 for supplier/product-integrity disruption and cross-company logistics context.
NPTEL-41 for the value of information in choices under uncertainty.
IITR-41 and GOOGLE-SLO for operational progress/control and service-target framing.
Then conduct the assigned scenario simulation and keep the executive decision log; no video substitutes for this exercise.
coveredTopics: Capacity planning and bottleneck context (NPTEL-08; NPTEL-30).
Supplier/product integrity and RFID/logistics disruptions as partial risk cases (MIT-06; MIT-13).
Production control/progress review and reliability targets (IITR-41; GOOGLE-SLO).
uncoveredTopics: A guided, integrated simulation combining an incident, capacity spike, supplier disruption, and executive decision log.
unitMap.practicalWork: Required learner-led fieldwork/simulation. Run the scenarios, make decisions, record evidence, owners, trade-offs, and executive rationale; academic viewing cannot replace the exercise.

remainingGaps: Unit 1: No verified video in this inventory teaches a complete current-state value-stream mapping method, including activity/queue/wait/lead-time and information-flow mapping; service-specific flow design also remains uncovered. Best partial coverage: NPTEL-01/NPTEL-35 and IITR-41 for broad operations flow; MIT-01/MIT-12 for IoT/RFID visibility; IITR-49 and GOOGLE-SLO for quality/reliability metrics.

Unit 2: Quantitative queueing theory and service waiting-time/variability analysis remain uncovered. Best partial coverage: NPTEL-08 demand/capacity planning and NPTEL-24/28/30 scheduling/bottlenecks.

Unit 2: The verified Google SLO lesson explains interaction measures, SLIs and SLO target-setting, but does not teach SRE error-budget policy or the release-speed/reliability trade-off. Error-budget implications therefore remain a gap.

Unit 3: No verified single lecture fully covers supplier/third-party concentration risk assessment, procurement contracts, strategic sourcing, or current cloud-provider concentration. Best partial coverage: inventory/safety-stock series NPTEL-09/14/16/20/21/23 and MIT-06/12/13 traceability, counterfeit and logistics examples.

Unit 4: No verified video develops an integrated technology-operations dashboard with owners, escalation thresholds, incident cadence, and economic/customer KPI design. Best partial coverage: IITR-41 production control, IITR-49 SPC/control charts, and GOOGLE-SLO reliability targets.

Unit 5: Explicit make/buy/platform-selection criteria and a contemporary technology-roadmap method are not fully taught by a directly mapped recording. Best partial coverage: NPTEL-36/37/38 network design and MIT-08 product lifecycle/automotive roadmap case.

Unit 6: No video can provide or replace the integrated incident/capacity-spike/supplier-disruption review simulation and executive decision log. This remains required learner work; NPTEL-08/30/41 and MIT-06/13 provide only academic decision context.

courses.title: Technology Finance, Capital Allocation, and Portfolio Decisions
courses.level: Graduate core. MIT 15.401 is a Sloan graduate finance course. The companion uses it for decision quality, not investment advice or a securities-trading plan.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra and willingness to work through present value, discounting, uncertainty, and sensitivity analysis. CTO-01 roadmap and CTO-05 unit economics are recommended.
objectives: Explain time value, risk, return, diversification, and capital-market concepts relevant to technology leaders.
Build NPV, scenario, and sensitivity models for technology investments.
Separate project value, portfolio correlation, option value, and financial affordability.
Challenge metrics that obscure uncertainty, technical debt, or non-financial risk.
Present a capital-allocation recommendation with assumptions, downside cases, and kill criteria.
units: Set finance vocabulary: cash flow, opportunity cost, discount rate, risk, and decision context.
Work present-value and fixed-income sessions; build a cash-flow model for one technology investment.
Study equities, forwards, futures, and options only to understand risk transfer and optionality, not to trade.
Study risk/return and portfolio theory; map correlated technology bets.
Study CAPM/APT and capital budgeting; perform sensitivity, scenario, and break-even analysis.
Study efficient markets and behavioral limitations; prepare an investment-committee memo.
courses.assignment: Build a transparent capital-allocation workbook and 4-page decision memo for a technology portfolio: cash flows, NPV, three scenarios, sensitivities, risk register, option/sequence logic, non-financial constraints, and fund/hold/stop recommendations.
courses.assessment: Use the stated rubric: analytical correctness and evidence 30%; application to the chosen organization 30%; decisions, trade-offs, and risk treatment 25%; clarity and executive communication 15%. A score of 80/100 is the self-study passing threshold.
mapping: R&D project definition, portfolio management, technology evaluation and finance
Management of Technology: Strategy and Portfolio Analysis
Budgeting for technology implementation and strategic priorities

lectures.title: Ses 1: Introduction and Course Overview
lectures.coverageNote: Finance framework, financial decision context and fundamental principles; primary sequence opening session.

lectures.title: Ses 2: Present Value Relations I
lectures.coverageNote: Asset cash flows through time, certainty and present-value operator.

lectures.title: Ses 3: Present Value Relations II
lectures.coverageNote: NPV calculations, annuities/perpetuities and compounding conventions.

lectures.title: Ses 4: Present Value Relations III & Fixed-Income Securities I
lectures.coverageNote: Concludes PV with inflation and real/nominal returns; begins fixed-income securities and coupon-bond valuation.

lectures.title: Ses 5: Fixed-Income Securities II
lectures.coverageNote: Spot/forward rates, yield curves, interest-rate expectations and term-structure models.

lectures.title: Ses 6: Fixed-Income Securities III
lectures.coverageNote: Coupon bond valuation, law of one price and interest-rate risk measures.

lectures.title: Ses 7: Fixed-Income Securities IV
lectures.coverageNote: Securitization and intermediation, sources of corporate-bond risk, payment priority and correlation.

lectures.title: Ses 8: Equities
lectures.coverageNote: Equities and dividend-discount valuation; use as market-finance context, not a recommendation to invest or trade.

lectures.title: Ses 9: Forward and Futures Contracts I
lectures.coverageNote: Contracts, uncertainty, illiquidity, counterparty risk and risk-transfer context.

lectures.title: Ses 10: Forward and Futures Contracts II & Options I
lectures.coverageNote: Forward/futures payoff and pricing followed by call/put option concepts and terms.

lectures.title: Ses 11: Options II
lectures.coverageNote: Option payoff diagrams, call/put strategies and volatility; financial options, not a standalone real-options project-valuation treatment.

lectures.title: Ses 12: Options III & Risk and Return I
lectures.coverageNote: Binomial option-pricing model plus statistical background and return-risk concepts.

lectures.title: Ses 13: Risk and Return II & Portfolio Theory I
lectures.coverageNote: Security risk/return measures and the portfolio/mean-variance framework; composite lecture.

lectures.title: Ses 14: Portfolio Theory II
lectures.coverageNote: Portfolio mean, variance, standard deviation and correlation.

lectures.title: Ses 15: Portfolio Theory III & The CAPM and APT I
lectures.coverageNote: Tangency portfolio/Sharpe ratio and first CAPM material; composite lecture.

lectures.title: Ses 16: The CAPM and APT II
lectures.coverageNote: Risk-adjusted discount rates, CAPM applications and security-market-line performance evaluation.

lectures.title: Ses 17: The CAPM and APT III & Capital Budgeting I
lectures.coverageNote: CAPM portfolio examples plus managerial NPV decision rule and project cash flows; composite lecture.

lectures.title: Ses 18: Capital Budgeting II & Efficient Markets I
lectures.coverageNote: NPV applications, project financing, profitability index, IRR and capital rationing; also starts efficient-markets theory.

lectures.title: Ses 19: Efficient Markets II
lectures.coverageNote: Behavioral finance, uncertainty aversion, rationality and emotion, human preferences and adaptive-markets discussion.

lectures.title: Ses 20: Efficient Markets III & Course Summary
lectures.coverageNote: CAPM limits and adaptive-markets implications in the financial crisis, followed by course review; composite session.

viewingSequence: MIT401-08 for equity valuation context.
MIT401-09 → MIT401-10 for forwards/futures concepts; MIT401-10 → MIT401-12 for financial-options vocabulary and pricing.
NYU-VAL-22 → NYU-VAL-23 for the managerial/real-options distinction and applications to staged projects, patents and expansion.
coveredTopics: forward/futures contract features, payoff/pricing and risk transfer
counterparty risk and illiquidity in contract context
calls, puts, payoff diagrams and binomial option pricing
real-option concepts of delay, expansion, abandonment and staged investment using public NYU faculty lectures
unitMap.practicalWork: The original boundary is preserved: these are conceptual tools for decision quality, not trading instruction or a securities recommendation. Learner must identify any defensible project options in their own context.

unitMap.text: Study risk/return and portfolio theory; map correlated technology bets.
viewingSequence: MIT401-12 → MIT401-13 for risk/return measures.
MIT401-13 → MIT401-14 → MIT401-15 for mean/variance, correlations, portfolio selection, tangency portfolio and Sharpe ratio.
coveredTopics: security return and statistical risk measures
unitMap.practicalWork: The videos teach financial-asset portfolios. Mapping covariance, concentration and diversification onto the learner's technology bets remains an applied portfolio exercise, not a video substitute.

unitMap.text: Study CAPM/APT and capital budgeting; perform sensitivity, scenario, and break-even analysis.
viewingSequence: MIT401-15 → MIT401-16 for CAPM/APT and risk-adjusted discount-rate concepts.
MIT401-17 → MIT401-18 for managerial NPV, project cash flows, IRR/profitability-index alternatives and capital rationing.
STRATH-01 for the narrower, shorter lesson on sensitivity, scenarios and break-even.
NYU-VAL-22 → NYU-VAL-23 for real-option valuation where staged commitments or flexibility matter; do not count this as ordinary NPV sensitivity analysis.
coveredTopics: capital budgeting and project NPV/cash flows
sensitivity analysis, scenario analysis and break-even analysis
real-option valuation as a supplement for contingent/staged investments
uncoveredTopics: technology-specific treatment of technical debt, cybersecurity/safety or other non-financial risk as a decision-model input; the finance series and supplements do not teach a CTO risk register or integrated financial/non-financial model governance
unitMap.practicalWork: Learner must build the sensitivity/scenario workbook, document assumptions and downside cases, set kill criteria, and explain non-financial constraints. The brief Strathclyde academic lesson is not a replacement for this hands-on analysis.

unitMap.text: Study efficient markets and behavioral limitations; prepare an investment-committee memo.
viewingSequence: MIT401-18 introduces efficient-markets theory after capital budgeting.
MIT401-19 for behavioral finance, uncertainty aversion and decision biases.
MIT401-20 for adaptive-markets implications and the course-wide finance review.
coveredTopics: behavioral-finance limits, preferences and uncertainty aversion
synthesis and review of the finance course
unitMap.practicalWork: The investment-committee memo is learner work. Videos do not draft the four-page recommendation, validate organizational facts, decide the fund/hold/stop allocation, or substitute for the stated assessment rubric.

remainingGaps: Internal technology-portfolio affordability and liquidity: no verified lecture in this set integrates runway, financing capacity and competing technology-capital commitments as constraints distinct from positive project NPV; fixed-income bond credit-risk and futures illiquidity lessons are only partial analogues.

CTO-specific technical-debt, cybersecurity/safety and other non-financial risk integration, plus model governance/validation against false precision: the videos provide finance/risk foundations and financial sensitivity methods, but no credible free full university lecture found in the targeted follow-up that teaches an integrated technology-capital model/risk register. Preserve this as learner research and judgment, not as covered lecture content.

Public archived lecture duration for the two NYU Session 22–23 supplements was not independently verified; duration_seconds is null. Their faculty course page links the individual YouTube recordings and names the relevant topics.

Unit 2: technology-portfolio affordability as an internal funding/cash-liquidity constraint (runway, competing capex commitments, funding availability) is not taught as a managerial financing module; fixed-income market credit/liquidity concepts are not a substitute

Unit 5: technology-specific treatment of technical debt, cybersecurity/safety or other non-financial risk as a decision-model input; the finance series and supplements do not teach a CTO risk register or integrated financial/non-financial model governance

courses.title: Technology Governance, Responsible AI, and Board Communication
courses.level: Full university business-ethics substitute plus the focused MIT AI-bias video and NIST governance readings.
courses.prerequisites: CTO-03 cyber charter, CTO-04 AI dossier, and CTO-08 capital-allocation memo.
objectives: Identify AI bias, transparency, accountability, safety, privacy, and contestability issues.
Turn AI RMF and CSF principles into accountable governance processes and evidence.
Define board-level technology, cyber, and AI reporting indicators without concealing uncertainty.
Set approval gates for high-impact models, agent permissions, changes, incidents, and exceptions.
Communicate residual risk, value, and ethical trade-offs in an executive-ready narrative.
units: Watch the full video in chapters I–III; define harms, stakeholders, and the limits of a purely technical “fix.”
Use chapters IV–V and the case prompts to articulate rights, fairness, and human-judgment questions.
Apply AI RMF GOVERN/MAP to policy, inventory, role, and impact-assessment controls.
Apply AI RMF MEASURE/MANAGE and CSF Govern to testing, monitoring, exceptions, and incident treatment.
Draft a board technology/AI/cyber scorecard: value, quality, safety, security, cost, compliance, and residual risk.
Complete capstone red-team review, revise governance gates, and deliver the final board presentation.
courses.assignment: Submit a 4–6 page governance charter and a 10-slide board pack covering AI/system inventory, material-use criteria, accountable owners, testing evidence, agent permissions, incident/exception decisions, metrics, and residual-risk acceptance.
courses.assessment: Use the stated rubric: analytical correctness and evidence 30%; application to the chosen organization 30%; decisions, trade-offs, and risk treatment 25%; clarity and executive communication 15%. A score of 80/100 is the self-study passing threshold.
mapping: Applied AI: ethics, governance, and responsible AI
Applied Agentic AI: governance, compliance, agent testing, and ethics
Impact project and executive-level strategic decisions

Equality and justice as distinct ethical questions

Use NPTEL L58–L59 as supplementary context on IT ethics, data identity, and security.

Fairness and algorithmic bias in AI pipelines
Ethical dimensions of data identity and security

Operational AI-system inventory, material-use thresholding, named model owners and impact-assessment evidence

unitMap.text: Apply AI RMF MEASURE/MANAGE and CSF Govern to testing, monitoring, exceptions, and incident treatment.

Use NIST AI RMF/CSF readings to fill the formal MEASURE/MANAGE and CSF Govern control detail.

uncoveredTopics: AI-specific testing protocols, continuous monitoring and model-change approval gates

Agent tool permissions, action limits, and agent-specific testing/monitoring

uncoveredTopics: An integrated board-level technology/AI/cyber scorecard with indicator definitions, trend/threshold design and uncertainty disclosure
